starNames.name: Hydor
starNames.origin: The IAU-name "Hydor" resembles the original application of this name as a constellation in a vast area of faint stars in antiquity. It fits nicely the Indigenous Arabian constellation of "Safina", Ship. Note that the name "Hydor" was misapplied to a star in Aqr in the recent time. WGSN corrects this mistake. The Greek term "Hydor" (Ὕδωρ), Water, originally referred to a huge constellation, depicted around Cetus on ancient globes and described south of Aquarius in Aratus's poem of the 4th century BCE.

starNames.name: Alpheratz
starNames.origin: The specific origin of this name is unclear. It may represent a transfer from β Peg, where alferaz and other variants were applied in medieval times as abbreviations for β Peg's Arabic name mankib al-faras, "the Horse's Shoulder". Or, it may be from an abbreviation of the name alpheraz id est equus, "alpheraz, that is, the Horse", which was applied directly to α And also in medieval times. In any case, Medieval Latin authors confused these two names, their spellings, and their identifications, and the modern application of "Alpheratz" to α And comes down to us from late medieval times.

starNames.name: Caph
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of its pre-Islamic Arabian name al-kaff al-khadib "the Stained Hand," alternatively and more correctly used for all the brighter stars of today's Cassiopeia (probably α, β, γ, δ, and ε). The pre-Islamic Arabian figure here represented a hand with its finger-tips stained reddish-brown in the traditional Eastern way using henna leaves. al-kaff al-khatdib, in turn, was part of the larger pre-Islamic Arabian asterism kaff althurayya al-yumna al-mabsuta, "the Outstretched Right Hand of the Pleiades." The latter extended from today's Taurus through Perseus into Cassiopeia. A second hand (the Pleiades were a "head" from which two arms or hands radiated) was al-kaff al-jadhma', "the Amputated Hand," in today's Cetus.

starNames.name: Tianjiu
starNames.origin: Tiān Jiù (天厩, Celestial Stable) is an ancient Chinese asterism. It is the heavenly counterpart to the imperial post-horse stations and cavalry stables on earth.

starNames.name: Algenib
starNames.origin: From the name for the Arabic Almagest period al-janb, "the Side," for α Per. Wrongly transferred to γ Peg in Early Modern times.

starNames.name: Simmakh
starNames.origin: Unlike most zodiac constellations, Pisces was not an ancient Mesopotamian constellation. Cuneiform literature calls this area SIM.MAḪ, The Swallow. WGSN picked a star that is inside its constellation area, despite transformations, at all times between 1400 and 100 BCE.

starNames.name: Ankaa
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the modern Arabic constellation name al-'anqa' (a fabulous bird) for Phoenix.

starNames.name: Cexing
starNames.origin: Cè (Whip, 策) is an ancient Chinese star name representing the horsewhip, located beside the asterism Wangliang (王良) and closely associated with both Wangliang (王良) and Tiansi (天駟). It belongs to the Gān school. "Xing" means star. The ancients sometimes also call it Cexing (whip star) or Tiance (celestial whip). In modern and postmodern literature in English, the name is occasionally used for γ Cas but this is a late shift, only attested from the 18th century onwards when the Chinese uranography was reworked under Jesuit influence. WGSN corrects the adoption to the Indigenous version.

starNames.name: Fulu
starNames.origin: traditional Chinese single star asterism: an auxiliary road to Gedao; also represents the chief assistant to maintain roads. Gedao (the flying corridor) is a long chain of stars next to the Purple Palace enclosure constellation. Paradoxically, the auxiliary road is considered a single star asterism as attested in several historical star charts (e.g. the famous Suzhou map). Sun and Kistemaker (1997) who studied sources from the Han dynasty (around the year "0" plusminus 200 years) identify ζ Cas with this single star. Another researcher, Sun Shuwei, who dealt with the Xinyixiangfayao Star Map from Su Song (苏颂, 1020-1101 CE) identifies δ Cas. Both is plausible.

starNames.name: Anunitu
starNames.origin: Anunītu (𒀭𒀀𒉡𒉌𒌓), the Heavenly, is a by-name for the goddess of love (and war) Inanna = Ištar in the Dynasty of Akkad (~2300 BCE) in Mesopotamia. She was represented by a constellation in the And/Psc-area.

starNames.name: Kuda
starNames.origin: Kuda is Malay and borrowed from Tamil குதிரை (kutirai), meaning horse. The constellation is used on the islands of Java and Bali where horses are considered a luxury item.

starNames.name: Schedar
starNames.origin: Applied with various spellings since medieval times, from the Arabic word al-sadr, "the breast," used in the Arabic Almagest in describing this star.

starNames.name: Diphda
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of its pre-Islamic Arabian name al-difdi' al-thani, "the Second Frog" (a PsA was the pre-Islamic Arabians' "First Frog," al-difdi' al-awwal).

starNames.name: Shimu
starNames.origin: "Tian Shi Mu", The Eye of the Celestial Pig, is the oldest preserved name for this star in China. Later, this region was named Kui, the Legs, and zeta And was (in historical times before Qing Dynasty) used as the determinative star of this constellation and lunar mansion.

starNames.name: Waiping
starNames.origin: Wài Píng (外屏, Outer Fence) is a traditional Chinese asterism belonging to the Kui (奎) mansion, whose name-giving constellation was called a pig (Shimu) in ancient times. The fence makes the pigsty unseen.

starNames.name: Achird
starNames.origin: The proper name Achird was apparently first applied to Eta Cassiopeiae in the Skalnate Pleso Atlas of the Heavens published in Slovacia in 1950, but is not known prior to that.

starNames.name: Tianhun
starNames.origin: Tiān Hùn (天溷), Celestial Pigsty, is a Chinese asterism and at least 2000 years old. It belongs to the Kui mansion, whose determining asterism was also called Shimu (Pig).

starNames.name: Castula
starNames.origin: Castula is Latin for a type of woman's tunic. Bayer (1603, Uranometria) attributes the name "castulum" to Nonius (Portugese scholar Pedro Nunez, 1502-1578), with the Greek alias ταινίαν for a ribbon.

starNames.name: Tiansi
starNames.origin: Tiān Sì (Heavenly Quadriga, 天駟) is an old Chinese asterism, attested for at least 2000 years. It comprises four of the five stars forming the constellation Wangliang (王良) and represents the four horses pulling the chariot. It may thus be regarded as a constituent sub-constellation/asterism of Wangliang (王良). In the literature in English, the name "Ce" (old spelling: Tsih) can be found; WGSN corrects this misapplication of an old star name.

starNames.name: Kui
starNames.origin: Kui奎, The Legs, is an ancient Chinese constellation with 16 stars, belonging to the 28 Lunar Mansions in China, with a very long history. Its determinative star used to be zeta And for many centuries but it was changed to eta And in Qing Dynasty.

starNames.name: Wurren
starNames.origin: Wurren is the Wardaman name of ζ Phe, from the Northern Territory, Australia. Wurren means “child” and refers to the “Little Fish”, a child of Dungdung – the life-creating Frog Lady. Wurren gives water to Gawalyan, the echidna (Achernar), which they direct Earthly initiates to carry in small bowls. The water came from a great waterfall used to cool the people during the ceremony. Just as the water at the base of the waterfall keeps people cool and rises to the sky as mist, the water in the initiates’ bowls keeps them cool and symbolically transforms into clouds that bring the wet rains of the monsoon season. These ceremonies occur in late December when the weather is hot and these stars are high in the evening sky, signalling the start of the monsoon.

starNames.name: Gajahmina
starNames.origin: Gajahmina is derived from the Sanskrit गज, gajah, elephant, and मीन, mīna, fish. The constellation name is preserved as a loanword in Balinese. Philosophically, the Gajah Mina shrine is a symbol of the tremendous power of the King of the Ocean, namely Dewa Baruna.

starNames.name: Tarandus
starNames.origin: Tarandus is an alternative name for the Early Modern European constellation "Rangifer", the Reindeer, from Greek τάρανδος (reindeer), Latinised by Carl Linnaeus 1758 "Cervus Tarandus" for a species, Jamieson 1822 used "Rangifer tarandus" for the reindeer in the sky.

starNames.name: Junnanmen
starNames.origin: Jūn Nán Mén (军南门, "Southern Millitary Gate") is a Chinese constellation, simplified: Junnanmen. It is the name of a Chinese single-star asterism that WGSN preserves in its earliest version (before Tang Dynasty), identified with φ And."Junnanmen" is assigned to the primary of the phi And (HR 335, HIP 5434, HD 6811) binary system, i.e. phi And A (HD 6811A).

starNames.name: Mirach
starNames.origin: Ultimately from the Arabic word al-mi)zar, "the girdle" or "loin cloth", used in the Arabic Almagest in describing this star. The correct transliteration of the word in the Medieval Latin Almagest was mizar, which was occasionally misspelled as mirac, mirat, etc. These corruptions, taken as proper names for β And, were correctly attributed to al-mi)zar by Early Modern scholars. Subsequently one of the misspellings, "Mirach", gained more popularity over the correct "Mizar", to beome the preferred modern name.

starNames.name: Revati
starNames.origin: Revatī is a Hindu mother goddess, in Sanskrit written रेवती. It is also the name of the 27th nakshatra and specifically the star ζ Psc. The Sun passing this star designates the beginning of a new (solar) year.

starNames.name: Paushna
starNames.origin: Pauṣṇa (पौष्ण) is another name for Revati, a goddess that names the 27th Vedic nakshatra.

starNames.name: Buranun
starNames.origin: The Sumerian name for the river Euphrates. Euphrates has been honoured with two constellations, independently invented in early modern Europe and ancient Mesopotamia. WGSN picked a star in the ancient constellation.

starNames.name: Adhil
starNames.origin: From the Arabic word al-dhail, "the hem of a robe or dress", used in the Arabic Almagest in describing 49 And and χ And, and transliterated in the Medieval Latin Almagest as adhil. This word was wrongly applied as a star name to ξ And in recent times.

starNames.name: Tiancang
starNames.origin: Tiān Cāng (天倉, Square Celestial Granary) is a Chinese asterism from the Shi school (~2000 years old).

starNames.name: Ruchbah
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of its name for the Arabic Almagest period rukbat dhat al-kursiy, "the Knee of the Lady of the Chair."

starNames.name: Titawin
starNames.origin: Titawin (also known as Medina of Tetouan) is a settlement in northern Morocco and UNESCO World Heritage Site. Historically it was an important point of contact between two civilizations (Spanish and Arab) and two continents (Europe and Africa) after the 8th century.

starNames.name: Idigna
starNames.origin: The Sumerian term for the Tigris river. Tigris has been honoured with two constellations, independently invented in early modern Europe and ancient Mesopotamia. WGSN picked a star in the ancient constellation.

starNames.name: Achernar
starNames.origin: Arabic name آخر النهر (āḫiru ʾn-nahr) meaning, the End of the River; originally used for θ Eri that was considered the end of the river in the ancient star catalog (Almagest).The name was transferred to α Eri in the Early Modern Era when the constellation was extended south to this new terminus.

starNames.name: Nembus
starNames.origin: Name appears in Bayer's (1603) Uranometria for Upsilon Per (later designated 51 And), which he states is of Arab origin, however the name appears to be Latin not Arabic. From the description it appears that the name appears to be connected with the adamntine harpe sword Perseus used to decapitate Medusa.

starNames.name: Dajiangjunbei
starNames.origin: 天大将军, “Celestial Grand General” is an important constellation in ancient China. As the determinative star was already named, WGSN named the northernmost star "The Northern one of The Great General" (Dajiangjunbei).

starNames.name: Torcular
starNames.origin: The traditional name Torcularis septentrionalis (northern wine press) was taken from the 1515 Almagest (Latin translation) and abbreviated.

starNames.name: Baten Kaitos
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from its name for the Arabic Almagest period batn qaitus, "the Sea Monster's Belly."

starNames.name: Mothallah
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Arabic constellation name al-muthallath, "the Triangle," for Triangulum.

starNames.name: Segin
starNames.origin: Name of unknown etymology from the "Atlas Coeli Skalnaté Pleso" of Czech astronomer Antonín Bečvář (1901-1965).

starNames.name: Sheratan
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Arabic lunar mansion name al-shara-tan, for β and γ Ari. The name means "two" of something, but the complete meaning is uncertain. Some Arabic authors suggested that it meant "the Two Signs", implying these stars as some kind of celestial indicator; others assumed it meant "the Two Horns", referring to the Arabic figure of al-hamals here.

starNames.name: Alnaamaat
starNames.origin: Al-Naʿāmāt (النَّعَامَات), “the ostriches”, is an Arabic asterism. The name is independently recorded by ibn Qutayba and al-Ṣūfī.

starNames.name: Zibbatu
starNames.origin: Zibbatu is Akkadian for The Tails, referring to the "Tails of the Swallow", an asterism in the Mesopotamian constellation of The Swallow (SIM.MAḪ), which has been used in the Astronomical Diaries of Babylon for many centuries BCE to describe planet positions in Pisces.

starNames.name: Alrescha
starNames.origin: From the pre-Islamic Arabian lunar mansion name al-risha', "the Cord," for β And. Wrongly transferred to α Psc in recent times. According to a Arabic source, the pre-Islamic Arabian al-risha' included, in a larger sense, two curving lines of mostly dim stars in Andromeda and Pisces, meant to attach to the pre-Islamic Arabian al-dalw "the Well Bucket" (marked by today's Square of Pegasus). It is also possible that this "cord" was a remnant of the cord joining the two fish of the older Babylonian zodiac. Indeed, these stars of the cord were alternatively known by the pre-Islamic Arabians as al-hut, "the Fish" (a single fish), corresponding to what in other cultures was Pisces among the zodiacal signs (and according to this tradition, the Fish's brightest star, β And, was batn al-hut, "the Fish's Belly").

starNames.name: Gang
starNames.origin: Gàng (“Shaft”) forms part of the ancient Chinese asterism of Huá Gài (Canopy of the Emperor, 華蓋). Allen (1899) mentions the term as a star name in Cam but WGSN places it in a correcter position.

starNames.name: Almach
starNames.origin: The formation of this name begins with the Arabic name for this star: ʿanaq al-ard, "the Caracal" (a black-eared feline predator found in the Middle East). The Arabs also gave the name in short form as al-ʿanaq, which became transliterated into Medieval Latin as alamac. Later, the derivatin of alamac was erroneously attributed to the assumed Arabic word al-maq (properly al-muq) for "the boot" or "buskin", rather than to al-ʿanaq. Subsequently the erroneous word, as "Almaak" and later "Almach" was applied as a star name to γ And, mostly in astronomical works in English. Other, non-English works use the spelling "Alamak" derived directly from the Medieval Latin transliteration.

starNames.name: Rangifer
starNames.origin: Rangifer, the Reindeer, is an extinct constellation first introduced by Pierre-Charles Le Monnier in 1743 in the book La Théorie des Comètes. He aimed to resemble an Indigenous constellation of the Sami people in Northern Scandinavia, where he had travelled to on a geodetic expedition.

starNames.name: Hamal
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Arabic constellation name, al-hamal, "the Lamb", for Aries. al-hamal seems to belong to those zodiacal constellation names already known in Arabic times.

starNames.name: Alaybasan
starNames.origin: Al-Aybasān (الأيبسان), the Two Joints (of bones), is an Indigenous Arabian asterism. Name variants are Al-Anīsān (الأنيسان) and Al-Baysan. The later spelling variant al-Anīsān that originated from a mistake changed the meaning, as it translates The Two Friends. WGSN adopts a spelling variant without hyphen: "Alaybasan" is the name for β Tri

starNames.name: Triminus
starNames.origin: The star ι Tri (iota or 6 Trianguli) is the brightest one in the early modern variant of a lesser triangle next to the recognisable classical asterism within the constellation Triangulum. The name is composed of the IAU-abbreviation "Tri" and Hevelius's name "Minus" for the lesser triangle. The name applies to the visible dot in the sky, so that "iot Tri A" is "Triminus A". The other component is not visible to the naked eye.

starNames.name: Zuogeng
starNames.origin: Zuǒ Gēng (左更, Official in Charge of the Forest) and Yòu Gēng (右更, Official in Charge of Pasturing) are two paired Chinese asterisms.

starNames.name: Bawy
starNames.origin: Bawy, bȝwy, the dual form of Ba (the Soul), i.e. Two Souls, is an Egyptian name, used in decanal star clocks (~2300 BCE).

starNames.name: Deltoton
starNames.origin: Deltoton (Δελτωτόν; the letter Delta: Δ) is an ancient Greek name variant for the constellation triangulum, probably the original one as "Delta" is the first letter in the ancient Greek term for "dios", the highest god who possesses and rules the stars. In early uranographies, this triangle was considered a sign of the divinity of the starry sky, a divine inscription "written in the stars".

starNames.name: Apdu
starNames.origin: Apd(w), ȝpd, The Bird, is an ancient Egyptian constellation from the second millennium BCE; the language is moribunt. There are at least 21 spelling variants throughout the millennia in hierglyphs, and it is probably not any specific bird; might be a goose or falcon or something else. Four star names within the constellation are attested in Ramesside Star Clocks and identified with the area between α, β Per and all of Triangulum. WGSN adopts the name of the constellation for any unspecific spot within its area to preserve an old Egyptian cultural name.

starNames.name: Mira
starNames.origin: Its Latin name since Early Modern times meaning "the Amazing One", as taken from Historiola Mirae Stellae - the title of a work describing the amazing variability of this star (written by Hevelius in 1662).

starNames.name: Chugao
starNames.origin: Chú Gǎo (蒭藁, Hay) is a Chinese asterism west of Tiānyuàn (天苑, Celestial Meadow) and is attested for more than 2000 years.

starNames.name: Huagai
starNames.origin: Huá Gài (Canopy of the Emperor, 華蓋) is a Chinese asterism consisting of sixteen stars, divided into two parts: seven stars forming the Huá Gài (“Canopy”) proper and nine forming the Gàng (“Shaft”). The asterism originated within the Gan school during the Han dynasty, around the first century BCE.

starNames.name: Polaris
starNames.origin: A Latin adjective meaning "of the pole" (related to the noun polus, "the pole"). Applied as a star name to α UMi in Early Modern times, it reflects the star's temporary proximity to the north celestial pole.

starNames.name: Kaffaljidhma
starNames.origin: Arabic الكف الجذماء, al-kaf al-jaðmāʾ ('the cut-short hand') is given as a star name in Allen (1899) with reference to an Arabic name for the asterism of Cetus's Head.

starNames.name: Weixiu
starNames.origin: Wèi (胃, Stomach), or Wèi Xiù (胃宿), is the seventeenth of the Chinese Twenty-Eight Mansions system. It marks the stomach of the super-constellation White Tiger.

starNames.name: Lilii Borea
starNames.origin: Lacaille used the now obsolete constellation Lilium (The Lily) and named this star "the northern one of the Lily", in Latin: Lilii Borea. see also "Lilium" in the ASE.

starNames.name: Bharani
starNames.origin: the Indian term (Sanscrit: भरणी), The Bearer, designates the 2nd of the 27 nakshatras consisting of the three stars 35, 39 and 41 Ari, among which 41 Ari is the brightest. The modern star name was given to the brightest star of the historical constellation.

starNames.name: Miram
starNames.origin: perhaps a misspelling of the Arabic term مِعْصَم miʽṣam, The Wrist, which was used for naming κ Per "Misam" in the CSN.

starNames.name: Angetenar
starNames.origin: derived from the Arabic Al Ḥināyat an-Nahr, 'the Bend in the River', based on Arabic Almagest translations

starNames.name: Azha
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism name udhi al-na'am, "the Ostrich's Nest," for ζ, ρ2,3, η and τ1 Eri, and ε and π Cet.

starNames.name: Acamar
starNames.origin: From its name for the Arabic Almagest period akhir al-nahr, "the River's End". Applied in medieval times, and reapplied in recent times

starNames.name: Menkar
starNames.origin: From the Arabic word al-minkhar, "the nostrils," used in the Arabic Almagest in describing λ Cet. Wrongly applied as a star name to α Cet (properly on the "jaw") in a Medieval Latin star table.

starNames.name: Algol
starNames.origin: Applied in medieval times from an abbreviation of its name for the Arabic Almagest period ras al-ghul "the Demon's Head" (for Ptolemy's Gorgon-head). "Algol" is one of the oldest Arabic star names applied in the West, from the end of the 10th century A.D.

starNames.name: Misam
starNames.origin: the Arabic term مِعْصَم miʽṣam, The Wrist, was originally a name of χ Per (Almagest: "the right hand" of the Hero) and considered the Wrist of Thurayya (the Pleiades) for the Arabs.

starNames.name: Botein
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the pre-Islamic Arabian lunar mansion name al-butain, "the Little Belly", for δ, ϵ and ρ Ari.

starNames.name: Shangcheng
starNames.origin: Shàng Chéng (The Great Imperial Minister, 上丞) and Shào Chéng (The Second Imperial Minister, 少丞) are the two stars located to the left and right of the northern gate of the Zǐ Gōng (Purple Palace) / Zǐwēi Yuán (Purple Enclosure).

starNames.name: Dalim
starNames.origin: The name was introduced for the star by Piazzi (1814) originating from the Indigenous Arabian asterism ظَلِيم al-ẓalīm, The Ostrich, seen in various stars (e.g. Fomalhaut, theta Eridani)

starNames.name: Zibal
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from a misreading of the pre-Islamic Arabian name al-ri'al, "the Young of the Ostriches," for the numerous dim stars running between α Eri and α PsA (or, according to another tradition, those within the triangle formed by α Phe/α PsA/β Cet).

starNames.name: Mirfak
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of its pre-Islamic Arabian name mirfaq al-thurayya, "the Elbow of the Pleiades," for its location in the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism here.

starNames.name: Ran
starNames.origin: Ran is the Norse goddess of the sea, who stirs up the waves and captures sailors with her net.

starNames.name: Sarvvis
starNames.origin: Sarvvis, the reindeer or moose (bull), is an Indigenous constellation, used by the Sami people of northern Scandinavia.

starNames.name: Rana
starNames.origin: Rana is Latin "The Frog". There are several stars named "frog" in the Arabic culture but at different places. WGSN placed the name at that constellation of the river.

starNames.name: Atik
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times (also to ζ Per), from an abbreviation of the pre-Islamic Arabian name 'atiq al-thurayya, "the Collarbone of the Pleiades," for ο and ζ Per, after their location in the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism here

starNames.name: Celaeno
starNames.origin: These names were individually applied in Early Modern times from a family of characters in Greek mythology: Atlas, Pleione and their seven daughters, the Pleiades.

starNames.name: Electra
starNames.origin: These names were individually applied in Early Modern times from a family of characters in Greek mythology: Atlas, Pleione and their seven daughters, the Pleiades.

starNames.name: Taygeta
starNames.origin: These names were individually applied in Early Modern times from a family of characters in Greek mythology: Atlas, Pleione and their seven daughters, the Pleiades.

starNames.name: Maia
starNames.origin: These names were individually applied in Early Modern times from a family of characters in Greek mythology: Atlas, Pleione and their seven daughters, the Pleiades.

starNames.name: Asterope
starNames.origin: These names were individually applied in Early Modern times from a family of characters in Greek mythology: Atlas, Pleione and their seven daughters, the Pleiades.

starNames.name: Merope
starNames.origin: These names were individually applied in Early Modern times from a family of characters in Greek mythology: Atlas, Pleione and their seven daughters, the Pleiades.

starNames.name: Alcyone
starNames.origin: These names were individually applied in Early Modern times from a family of characters in Greek mythology: Atlas, Pleione and their seven daughters, the Pleiades.

starNames.name: Atlas
starNames.origin: These names were individually applied in Early Modern times from a family of characters in Greek mythology: Atlas, Pleione and their seven daughters, the Pleiades.

starNames.name: Pleione
starNames.origin: These names were individually applied in Early Modern times from a family of characters in Greek mythology: Atlas, Pleione and their seven daughters, the Pleiades.

starNames.name: Custos
starNames.origin: Custos Messium, the Harvest Keeper, was a constellation invented in Early Modern Time by the French astronomer Joseph Jérôme de Lalande (1732–1807) who might have punned with the name of his compatriot Charles Messier. Some European astronomers copied and translated it, though. The constellation became obsolete in the depolitisation of the IAU-sky and WGSN only resembles the Keeper, Custos.

starNames.name: Shaowei
starNames.origin: Shào Wèi (The Second Imperial Guard, 少衛) is the sixth star on the right wall of the Zǐ Gōng (Purple Palace, 紫宮) or Zǐwēi Yuán (Purple Forbidden Enclosure), counting northward from the southern gate. Although its identification has varied across historical sources, all recorded versions consistently place it within the modern constellation Camelopardalis.

starNames.name: Áldu
starNames.origin: Áldu, the Reindeer Cow, in Sami language. The Sami constellation of the reindeer is usually called with the male term "Sarvvis", but mythology reports it keeping its antlers during winter, which only females do.

starNames.name: Zaurak
starNames.origin: From the Arabic word zauraq, "boat," used in an unaginat1ve, nonclassical description of several stars near Eridanus (evidently the stars of today's Phoenix). Arbitrarily applied as a star name toy Eri in recent times.

starNames.name: Menkib
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of its pre-Islamic Arabian name mankib al-thurayya, "the Shoulder of the Pleiades," for its location in the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism here.

starNames.name: Bibing
starNames.origin: Bibing (畢柄), The handle of the Net (Lunar Mansion) in the super-constellation of the White Tiger of the West, attested in ancient China for more than 2000 years.

starNames.name: Beid
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the pre-Islamic Arabian name al-baid, "the Eggs" for unspecified dim stars around the pre-Islamic Arabian ostrich's nest.

starNames.name: Rhombus
starNames.origin: Lacaille named the constellation ''Réticule Rhomboïde'' which may refer to the earlier constellation "Rhombus" that Habrecht (1621) defined in the area.

starNames.name: Keid
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the pre-Islamic Arabian name al-qaid, "the Egg Shells," for unspecified stars around the pre-Islamic Arabian ostrich's nest.

starNames.name: Prima Hyadum
starNames.origin: the Latin term occurs first in Flamsteed (1729) but is based on the Arabic idea to enumerate the stars in the cluster; in Arabic it was Awwal ad-Dabarān, The First of Dabarān (the group from which the star name "Aldebaran" derives).

starNames.name: Secunda Hyadum
starNames.origin: The Latin term Hyadum II goes back to Flamsteed (1729) in analogy to Hyadum I or Prima Hyadum

starNames.name: Beemim
starNames.origin: Spelling variations of this name appeared in medieval sources for star 29 in Eridanus in the Almagest (Upsilon3 Eri), with the Alfonsine Tables (1492, Tabule Astronomice Alfonsi Regis) spelling it as "Beemim".

starNames.name: Shakata
starNames.origin: Rohiṇīśakaṭa (रोहिणीशकट) is the Cart of Rohini, a deity represented in the star Aldebaran, and one of the nakshatras. Her cart is traditionally seen in the Hyades star cluster; WGSN represents it by a star within their central area to honour the area's cultural importance.

starNames.name: Ain
starNames.origin: From an abbreviation of the name for the Arabic Almagest period ain al-thaur "the Bull's Eye," for a Tau. Applied to ε Tau in recent times (Ptolemy had α Tau the southern eye, and ε Tau on the northern eye).

starNames.name: Chamukuy
starNames.origin: The Yucatec Maya identify Theta Tauri as chamukuy, the name of a small bird.

starNames.name: Theemin
starNames.origin: The formation of this name begins with one of the words used by Ptolemy to describe this star in the Almagest: καμπή, "the bend [of the river]". This was misread by the Arabs, who transliterated the word as bhmn. This, in turn, was transliterated as beemun in the Medieval Latin Almagest, which was corrupted to beemin, beemim, etc. Then in Early Modern times, the derivation of the form beemim was erroneously attributed to the Hebrew word te'omim, "twins." Subsequently this erroneous word, written as Theemim, then "Theemin," was applied as a star name to any of the various dim stars running from u1 to h Eri.

starNames.name: Aldebaran
starNames.origin: Applied in the early Islamic period from its pre-Islamic Arabian name al-dabaran, possibly meaning "the Follower," alternatively used as the lunar mansion name for all the Hyades (or again for α Tau alone). The name is thought to refer to this star's following the Pleiades across the sky, or to the Hyades (or α Tau) coming after the Pleiades as a lunar mansion. "Aldebaran" is one of the oldest Arabic star names applied in the West, from the end of the 10th century A.D.

starNames.name: Sceptrum
starNames.origin: from the obsolete constellation of Sceptrum Brandenburgicum

starNames.name: Gaja
starNames.origin: The term "gaja" (गज) in Sanskrit means "elephant". Yet, the constellation "Gaja(h)" is not known in India but only in Indonesia. There it is attested in the cultural calendar called Palelintangan where it is found in the intersection between Sunday and the second day of a five-day cycle.

starNames.name: Tabit
starNames.origin: Arabic الثابت al-thābit 'the endurer (the fixed/constant one)'

starNames.name: Lembu
starNames.origin: "Lintang Lěmbu" means Ox/Bull/Cow Constellation, representing an animal to pull carts & chariots. It is found in the calendar series Palelintangan used for at least 1300 years on the islands of Java and Bali, Indonesia.

starNames.name: Hassaleh
starNames.origin: hasa means in Arabic - handsome or good or benefactor, hassa (with doubled s) is from the same Arabic root, has long vowel (second a) and its meaning is "doer of good" or "benefactor", the end of name "-eh" (or "-ah") could mean femininum. Name from the "Atlas Coeli Skalnaté Pleso" of Czech astronomer Antonín Bečvář (1901-1965).

starNames.name: Almaaz
starNames.origin: The Arabic term المعز (al-maʽaz) can refer to the plural "goats" but has also been interpreted as a He-Goat (contrasting Capella, the She-Goat). Allen (1899, 90) cites Hyde's 1665 translation of Ulugh Beg with this term for a group of stars (asterism or sub-constellation) in Auriga.

starNames.name: Saclateni
starNames.origin: Eta and Zeta Aurigae, the 8th and 9th stars of Auriga in the Almagest, were referred to as "the kids" - Eriphoi (Greek), Haedi (Latin), al-Jadayain (Arabic; al-Sufi). Hyginus (Poetica Astronomica, 2. 13) mentions the Greek astronomer Cleostratus of Tenedos (5th cen. BC) pointed out "the kids" among the stars. "Saclateni" appeared in the Alfonsine Tables ("Tabule astronomice Alfonsi Regis", 1492 print) and may be a corrupted Latinization of the Arabic Gadi-thani, "second kid" (Mesnard 1949, "Les noms arabes d'étoiles", Ciel et Terre, Vol. 65, p. 70)

starNames.name: Ping
starNames.origin: Píng (屏), the Screen in front of a toilet, is a Chinese constellation

starNames.name: Haedus
starNames.origin: The Almagest star catalogue gives for n Aur: τῶν ἑπι τοῦ ἀριστεροῦ καρπού β καλοvμένων Ἐρίϕωv ὁ ἑπόμενος (The rearmost of the two stars on the left wrist, which are called 'Haedi'). The Latin term "Haedi" is a translation of Greek Ἐρίϕωv and plural of "Haedus" meaning "young goat(s)".

starNames.name: Cursa
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism name kursiy al-jauza' al-muqaddam, "the Foremost footstool of aljauza' [today's Orion]," for λ, β and ψ Eri, and τ Ori.

starNames.name: Mago
starNames.origin: Mago is a National Park in Ethiopia noted for its giraffes. The star also happens to be in the constellation of Camelopardis (the giraffe).

starNames.name: Bade
starNames.origin: Bade, the Funeral Tower, is an Oceanic constellation name from Bali (Indonesia).

starNames.name: Rigel
starNames.origin: From an abbrevation of its pre-Islamic Arabian (and Arabic) name rijl al-jauza', the Foot of al-jauza'." "Rigel" is one of the oldest Arabic star names applied in the West, from the end of the 10th century A.D.

starNames.name: Capella
starNames.origin: Its ancient Roman name meaning "the She-goat" (but more commonly given, in antiquity, as Capra), after the star's Greek name αίξ, "the Goat". Reapplied in recent times. The Roman names Capella, Aselli (for γ/ δ Cnc), and others in the diminutive form (also in Greek), are likely meant to indicate an atypical use of words, as an animal's name given to a star instead of to the animal (rather than meaning "small" animals or personages).

starNames.name: Bellatrix
starNames.origin: A Latin name meaning "the Female Warrior", given to α Aur in a medieval astrological text (the reason behind this initial application is not fully understood and awaits further findings in corresponding Arabic texts). In late medieval times, bellatrix was transferred to γ Ori, perhaps by association with the name Bellator, "the Male Warrior", which was used for Orion in other astrological texts.

starNames.name: Elnath
starNames.origin: From the pre-Islamic Arabian name al-naṭh, "the Butting (with the horns)," an alternative name for the 1st lunar mansion al-sharaṭān consisting of β and γ Ari (see β Ari). Some late Arabic authors also applied al-naṭh as a star name to α Ari. In recent times the name, as “Nath,” was wrongly transferred to β Tau, and subsequently it was completed to “Elnath” (adding the Arabic definite article).

starNames.name: Nihal
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism name al-nihal "the Camels Beginning to Quench Their Thirst" for α, β, γ and δ Lep.

starNames.name: Mintaka
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of the pre-Islamic Arabian (and Arabic) asterism name mintaqat al-jauza', "the Belt (or Girdle) of al-jauza'", for δ, ε, and ζ Ori.

starNames.name: Arneb
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Arabic constellation name al-arnab "the Hare", for Lepus.

starNames.name: Meissa
starNames.origin: From the pre-Islamic Arabian name al-maisan, for either γ or ξ Gem. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It may mean "the Sparkling One," referring to a star, or "the Proudly Marching One," referring to a person. Together, γ and ξ Gem composed the pre-Islamic Arabian 6th lunar mansion alhan'a. The nearby stars λ, ϕ1, and ϕ2 Ori composed the adjacent 5th lunar mansion al-haq'a. Due to confusion between these two parent lunar mansions in a late Arabic source, "Meissa" was wrongly applied to λ Ori (rather than to γ or ξ Gem) in recent times. "Meissa" (without n at the end) corresponds to pre-Islamic Arabian almaisa', a variant form of al-maisan.

starNames.name: Hatysa
starNames.origin: Name of unknown etymology from the "Atlas Coeli Skalnaté Pleso" of Czech astronomer Antonín Bečvář (1901-1965).

starNames.name: Alnilam
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism name al-nizam, "the String of Pearls," for δ, ε, and ζ Ori.

starNames.name: Tianguan
starNames.origin: Chinese single star asterism, a celestial pass along the ecliptic which opens and closes

starNames.name: Phact
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Arabic word fakhita, "ring dove," used in connection with the constellation Cygnus in a Early Modern discussion of Arabic bird names.

starNames.name: Alnitak
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism name nitaq al-jauza, "the Belt (or Girdle) of al-jauza," for δ, ε, and ζ Ori.

starNames.name: Darlugal
starNames.origin: Derived from Sumerian DAR.LUGAL, The Rooster, an animal first domesticated in China and India, and archaeologically attested in West Asia only since the 2nd millennium BCE for cockfights.

starNames.name: Saiph
starNames.origin: From an abbreviation of the Arabic asterism name saif al-jabbar, the Giant's Sword," for η, c, θ, and ι Ori. Wrongly applied as a star name to κ Ori in recent times.

starNames.name: Wazn
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from some pre-Islamic Arabian name al-wazn, of unknown significance.

starNames.name: Betelgeuse
starNames.origin: Applied with varied spellings since medieval times, from its pre-Islamic Arabian name yad al-jauza', "the Hand of al-jauza'" (The first medieval transliteration into Latin was bedalgeuze, mistaking the initial Arabic letter as "b" instead of "y." In Early Modern times this corruption was erroneously attributed to the assumed Arabic word "bat" [properly ibt], for "the Armpit" of al-jauza', giving rise to the corruption Betelgeuse" seen today. Thus by Early Modern times both the "y" and "d" of the first part of the pre-Islamic Arabian name had become corrupted.) The pre-Islamic Arabian asterism al-jauza' was a feminine figure represented in the stars of what is today Orion. The origin of its name is unclear (as with nearly all of the ancient group of pre-Islamic Arabian names). The root jwz can mean "middle," and the word al-jauza' is structured as a feminine adjective, thus al-jauza' may mean "the female one, having something about her related to the middle." There have been different speculations as to what the "middle" reference, if that is what it is, could be (for one example). The pre-Islamic Arabians' al-jauza' corresponded to what in other cultures was Gemini among the zodiacal signs. The Arabics subsequently used the indigenous name for both the Greek Orion and Twins, leading to some confusion in star names between the two constellations. An alternative name for the Arabic Almagest period for Orion was al-jabbar, "the Giant" and for Gemini, al-taw'aman, "the Twins."

starNames.name: Bagu
starNames.origin: Bā Gǔ (Eight Kinds of Crops, 八穀) is a Chinese constellation consisting of eight stars located within the constellations Lynx, Auriga, and Camelopardalis. It refers to land management officials in charge of rice, millet, barley, wheat, soybean, bean, chestnut, and hemp. It belongs to the asterisms introduced by Gan De and originated during the Han dynasty (roughly 2000 years ago).

starNames.name: Menkalinan
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from its Arabic name mankib dhi l-(inan, "the Shoulder of the Reinholder".

starNames.name: Mahasim
starNames.origin: Arabic المِعْصَم al-miʽşam "the wrist", was used for λ Her by Bayer by misreading the Almagest (and its 1515 Latin translation) where the wrist is designated o Her. Allen 1899, 245 mentions that the 16th century Latin Almagest translation used the (misspelled) variant “Mahasim” for θ and η Aurigae.

starNames.name: Elkurud
starNames.origin: Early Arab poets referred to a number of anonymous stars as الفرود al-furūd, "the solitary ones". Besides this known name, Allen (1899) suggested that al-furūd might have been an old transcriber's error for القرود al-qurūd "the apes", which he rendered "Al Ḳurūd". Although this idea did not receive scholarly support, WGSN used the rare transliteration Elkurud for this star, as "Furud" was already chosen for ζ CMa.

starNames.name: Hoerikwaggo
starNames.origin: the name of the constellation originally was Mons Mensae (Table Mountain) and not only "table"; this mountain had been called Sea-Mountain by Indigenous ethnics, in the Saan/ Khoe language spelled Huriǂoaxa, simplified in Africaans Hoerikwaggo.

starNames.name: Propus
starNames.origin: Applied in Early Modern times from the Greek word πρόπους, "forward foot", used by Ptolemy in the Almagest in describing this star.

starNames.name: Shangwei
starNames.origin: Shàng Wèi (The Great Imperial Guard, 上衛) is the name of the fifth star on the right wall and the sixth star on the left wall of the Zǐ Gōng (Purple Palace, 紫宮) / Zǐwēi Yuán (Purple Forbidden Enclosure, 紫微垣), counting northward from the southern gate. Its corresponding star has changed many times throughout history.

starNames.name: Furud
starNames.origin: Ultimately from the Arabic word al-furud, "the solitary ones", used in an Arabic poet's allusion to anonymous "solitary stars" around some star hadari. The word was not intended as a name for specific stars as some later Arabic authors supposed. The attempted identity of the "al-furud" stars, like their companion hadari, was variously attributed to stars in today's Centaurus and Columba. The latter stars were included under Canis Maior in the Almagest, leading, in recent times, to the confused assignment of the erroneous "Furud".

starNames.name: Mirzam
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from its Arabic name al-mirzam, of unknown meaning. The Arabs also gave the name to β CMi, and sometimes to γ Ori. Each al-mirzam star preceded the rising of a brighter star (our Sirius, Procyon, and Betelgeuse, respectively), which probably connects to the unknown meaning.

starNames.name: Tejat
starNames.origin: From the Arabic word tihyat, said to be the singular form of al-tahayi, an pre-Islamic Arabian name of unknown meaning and disputed identification. In some sources, the plural al-tahayi is assigned to η, μ, and v Gem. As originally applied in recent times, η was "Tejat Prior," and μ was Tejat Posterior."

starNames.name: Canopus
starNames.origin: From its ancient Greek name Κάνωβος (Ptolemy's spelling), an untranslated proper name that was introduced rather late into Greek astronomy (perhaps in the 2nd century BCE). There seem to be Egyptian influences in the name's development. Reapplied in Early Modern times.

starNames.name: Alhena
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the pre-Islamic Arabian lunar mansion name al-bana, possibly meaning "the Mark on the Neck of a Camel," for γ and ξ Gem, or alternatively for γ, ξ, η, μ, and v Gem.

starNames.name: Pipit
starNames.origin: Among the Kendayan (Dayak Kenayatn) people of West Kalimantan province, Borneo, Indonesia, the star ν Pup is identified as "Pipit".

starNames.name: Kamelos
starNames.origin: "Kamelos" is Greek for camel, a pun with the name of the constellation "Camelopardalis" whose Latin term is a Greek loanword, literally meaning "checkered camel" = giraffe. On this base, Jacob Bartsch proposed 1624 "Camelus Rebeccae" as an alternative name for the constellation Camelopardalis, a reference to the story of Abraham's daughter-in-law, Rebecca.

starNames.name: Mebsuta
starNames.origin: From an abbreviation of the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism name dhira' al-asad almabsuta, "the Lion's Outstretched Paw," for one of the two pairs α/β Gem or α/β CMi. These pairs were assigned to the larger pre-Islamic Arabian asterism al-asad, but there is no unanimity in the Arabic sources as to which pair was the "outstretched" or "folded" paw. "Mebsuta" was arbitrarily applied as a star name to ε Gem in recent times. In its indigenous location stretching from parts of Gemini all the way into Virgo, the pre-Islamic Arabian al-asad, "the Lion," corresponded to what in other cultures was Leo among the zodiacal signs. Subsequently the Arabs used the indigenous name for the smaller Greek Lion (Leo).

starNames.name: Sirius
starNames.origin: From its ancient Greek name Σείριος, "the Scorching one", or "Brilliant One", appropriate for this brightest of the fixed stars. Reapplied in Early Modern times.

starNames.name: Alzirr
starNames.origin: Arabic الزِرّ , al-zirr, "the button". Allen (1899) attributes the name to Al Birūnī and it certainly does not have Greek roots as it is located at the foot of the eastern Twin.

starNames.name: Adhara
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Arabic asterism name al-'adhara, "the Virgins", for ε, δ, η and ο2 CMa. The significance of the name is unknown.

starNames.name: Tonglingxing
starNames.origin: Tóng Líng (Phoenix Tree Mound, 桐陵) is a traditional Chinese star name at the right wall of the Purple Palace constellation, rarely used, but ~2000 years old. WGSN uses "Tonglingxing" to avoid confusion with an asteroid name.

starNames.name: Citalá
starNames.origin: Citalá means River of stars in the native Nahuat language.

starNames.name: Nganurganity
starNames.origin: Nganurganity [ˈŋanuɾˌɡ̊aniɟ̊] is the "Jacky lizard" in the culture of the Boorong, a clan of the indigenous Maligundidj people of northwestern Victoria in Australia, who saw it as an ancestral figure who fights the moon, flanked by two wives, represented by stars on either side of him (δ CMa and ε CMa). The Moon is Mityan, the quoll. Mityan fell in love with one of the wives of Unurgunite and tried to lure her away. Unurgunite discovered Mityan’s trickery and attacked him, leading to a great fight in which Mityan was defeated. The Moon has been wandering the heavens ever since, the scars of the battle still visible on his face as maria. One of the wives (δ CMa) lies further away from Unurgunite and is closer to the Moon than the other wife (ε CMa). This is the wife Mityan tried to lure away. The name was listed as Unurgunite in Stanbridge(1857/61), for initial ng-, which does not occur in English, was typically ignored in transcription of that era. WGSN corrects the spelling.

starNames.name: Muliphein
starNames.origin: The formation of this name begins with the Arabic names hadari and al-wazn. In Arabic discussions of these names it came to be said that they were muhlifan, meaning "two [things] causing dispute [in this case as to these stars' identification] and the swearing of an oath". From this usage, al-muhlifan was wrongly taken as a name for hadari and al-wazn together. Transliterated and further mutilated as "Muliphein", the name was arbitrarily applied to the single star γ CMa in recent times.

starNames.name: Mekbuda
starNames.origin: From an abbreviation of the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism name dhira' al-asad al-maqbuqa, "the Lion's Folded Paw". Arbitrarily applied as a star name to ζ Gem in recent times.

starNames.name: Wezen
starNames.origin: From the Arabic name al-wazn, for one of a pair of stars, the other one being hadari. Arabic authors ventured to identify these stars as α/β Cen or α/β Col, but exactly what two stars were originally intended, and the significance of their names, is unknown. As a common noun in Arabic, al-wazn means "the weight". "Wezen" was arbitrarily applied to δ CMa in recent times.

starNames.name: Wasat
starNames.origin: From the Arabic word wasat, "middle," used by a Arabic commentator who was speculating on the meaning of the pre-Islamic Arabian constellation name al-jauza'. Reference was made to al-jauza's being in the "middle" (wasat) of the sky (perhaps meaning the celestial equator). The reference was intended to apply to the pre-Islamic Arabian figure located in today's Orion, however it was under the constellation which is today Gemini that the reference appeared (note the confusion between Orion and Gemini mentioned under α Ori). Therefore, after transliteration into Latin, it was in Gemini (to δ) that the word "Wasat" was arbitrarily applied as a star name in recent times.

starNames.name: Aludra
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the alternative Arabic asterism name al-(udhra, "the Virginity", and (udhrat aljauza), "the Virginity [?] of al-jauza)", for ε, δ, η and ο2 CMa. The name (udhrat al-jauza), by tying it with the nearly Arabic asterism al-jauza) (today's Orion), may have been an attempt to apply significance to the enigmatic and perhaps older name al-(udhra.

starNames.name: Gomeisa
starNames.origin: From the pre-Islamic Arabian surname al-ghumaisa', "the Little Bleary-eyed One ('with a filthy fluid in the corner of the eye')," for α CMi. Wrongly transferred to β CMi in recent times. The original significance of the surname is unknown. Perhaps as an attempt to explain the significance of al-ghumaisa', as well as that of the surname al-<abur, "the One Having Crossed Over [a river, etc.]," for α CMa, an Arabic fable developed associating these and other equally enigmatic star names. According to one version of the fable, al-ghumaisa and ai-'abur were sisters, and their brother was suhail (α Car). Suhail, in turn, was the suitor of al-jauza' (the feminine pre-Islamic Arabian figure in place of Orion). In coitus, suhail broke the spine of al-jauza', thus killing her, after which suhail fled south. He was followed by his sister al-'abur who "crossed over" the Milky Way (where the two stars now lie in the southern sky). Meanwhile suhail's second sister, al-ghumaisa, was left alone north of the Milky Way, weeping, until her "eyes became bleary." (The pre-Islamic Arabian name for α CMa was al-shi'ra, of unknown meaning. Apparently it was developed into a dualis form, al-shi'rayan, to accomodate both α CMa and α CMi, with the aforementioned "surnames" distinguishing the two.)

starNames.name: Castor
starNames.origin: From its ancient Greek name Κάστωρ, a character in Greek mythology, the twin of Pollux (β Gem). Reapplied in Early Modern times.

starNames.name: Jishui
starNames.origin: traditional Chinese single star asterism: translations of the term are "Bilgewater", "a store of water to make wine", or "accumulated water (held in by dikes for future use)". It refers to a faint star in Gemini or Perseus that is idenfied differently by modern authors. Sun and Kistemaker (1997) from Han sources and Sun Shuwei (Stellarium) from a medieval source both suggest o Gem while Xu et al. (2000) identify lambda Persei.

starNames.name: Procyon
starNames.origin: From its ancient Greek name Προκύων, "the One Preceding the Dog", referring to its rising shortly before the "Dog Star", Sirius. Reapplied in Early Modern times.

starNames.name: Pollux
starNames.origin: This is the classical Latin form of its ancient Greek name Πολυδεύκης, a character in Greek mythology, the twin of Castor (α Gem). Reapplied in Early Modern times.

starNames.name: Azmidi
starNames.origin: The name is an abbreviated misspelling of a Greek term. In the Almagest, the third star in Argo is called "The northernmost of the 2 stars close together over the little shield in the poop." The 'little shield' in Greek is ἀσπιδίσκῃ (Aspidiske), sometimes misspelled Azmidi(ske), and the asterism may or may not consist of stars, while the Almagest lists ξ and ο Pup "above" it. According to Allen (1899) The Century Atlas (1897) by Benjamin E. Smith registers ι Arg (now Car) with the name "Aspidiske".

starNames.name: Naos
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the word ναῦς, Greek for the "ship", used in one Early Modern discussion as a name for the ancient constellation Argo (since divided into Puppis, Carina, and Vela).

starNames.name: Tureis
starNames.origin: From the Arabic word al-turais, "the Little Shield," used in the Arabic Almagest in describing several stars (ρ Pup not among them) in the constellation Argo. Wrongly applied as a star name to ρ Pup in recent times.

starNames.name: Tegmine
starNames.origin: A Latin word in the ablative case meaning "covering" or "shell" (nominative case would be "tegmen"), used in a Early Modern discussion of the constellation Cancer. The word was subsequently applied as a star name to ζ Cnc.

starNames.name: Tarf
starNames.origin: Arabic: الطرف, Al-Ṭarf (The eyes of the lion) is one of the traditional "Lunar Stations". It is composed of the 2 stars: ε Leo and ο Leo. However, the name has been in common use for β Cnc as it was published in the Yale Bright Star Catalogue.

starNames.name: Piautos
starNames.origin: piautos (πιαυτος) is a composition from Greek autos ("self") and Coptic pi- ("that") meaning "the same one". It occurred in a Coptic manuscript on lunar stations. Coptic is the ancient Egyptian language written in Greek letters, but lunar stations were uncommon for both the Greek and Egyptian culture. Hence, the origin of this term remains unknown.

starNames.name: Avior
starNames.origin: Invented for The Air Almanac of the HM Nautical Almanac Office

starNames.name: Alsciaukat
starNames.origin: misspelled Arabic الشوكة aš-šawkat (al-shaukat), The Thorn. The name obviously has nothing to do with the figure of the lynx (or historically sometimes called "Tiger" or "Tigris") that was invented in Early Modern Times.

starNames.name: Muscida
starNames.origin: Almagestum 1515: "illa quae est supra extremitatem Musciae" - Bayer (1603) "in naso, barbaris muscida." - attributed to "Barbarians"

starNames.name: Minchir
starNames.origin: Minchir appeared in Bode's 1801 Uranographia rooting in the Arabic term منخر الشجاع minkhar ash-shujāʽ "the nostril brave one" in Hydra.

starNames.name: Meleph
starNames.origin: Bayer (1603) quotes Arabic designations Melleff and Meeleph for this star (among others) which was adopted by other astronomers (e.g. Riccioli) and goes back to the Arabic term Al Ma'laf, The Stall (a variant of the Greek Manger).

starNames.name: Asellus Borealis
starNames.origin: From their joint Roman name the Aselli (and also Asini), "the Asses" of "Donkeys", being a translation of these stars' Greek name. Reapplied in Early Modern times, along with the Latin distinctions of "northern" and "southern".

starNames.name: Asellus Australis
starNames.origin: From their joint Roman name the Aselli (and also Asini), "the Asses" of "Donkeys", being a translation of these stars' Greek name. Reapplied in Early Modern times, along with the Latin distinctions of "northern" and "southern".

starNames.name: Alsephina
starNames.origin: The term is Arabic for "The Ship". It originates from the translation of Greek knowledge to Arabic when Argo Navis (The Ship Argo) was translated to Arabic and, thus, originally referred to the whole constellation rather than any specific star.

starNames.name: Yuyu
starNames.origin: Yuyu is a word from Javanese, inherited from Old Javanese "hayuyu", spoken on the island of Java, Indonesia. It means "freshwater crab". The animal can be found in rice fields in Indonesia and the constellation is attested for at least 1300 years.

starNames.name: Ashlesha
starNames.origin: Āśleṣā (आश्लेषा) is the Sanskrit name for an asterism in Hydra. It is considered one of the traditional Nakṣatras (lunar stations).

starNames.name: Copernicus
starNames.origin: Nicolaus Copernicus or Mikolaj Kopernik (1473-1543) was a Polish astronomer who proposed the heliocentric model of the solar system in his book "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium".

starNames.name: Acubens
starNames.origin: Applied with various spellings since medieval times, from the Arabic word al-zubana, "the claw", used in Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos in describing the stars α and ι Cnc. Otherwise, the same Arabic word was used for the "claws" of Scorpius.

starNames.name: Talitha
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of the pre-Islamic Arabian name alqafza al-thalitha, "the Third Leap," for ι and κ UMa. This pair, with the pairs λ/μ and v/ξ UMa, composed the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism qafazat al-ziba', "the Leaps of the Gazelles," imagined as the tracks left by those animals. In some later tradition, qafazat al-ziba' and adjacent asterisms were associated in a fable, where several gazelles leaped away from the Lion into a pond, leaving their tracks behind.

starNames.name: Alkaphrah
starNames.origin: corrupted spelling of Arabic القفزة al-qafzah "the leap" of the Indigenous Arabic group of gazelle asterisms preserved in Ibn Qutaybah.

starNames.name: Suhail
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times and representing an abbreviation of any of several composite pre-Islamic Arabian names (for example suhail al-wazn, suhail al-muhlif) that Arabic authors variously attributed to brighter stars in the region of suhail. A Vel was among these brighter stars. Some of the composite names may have been authentic pre-Islamic Arabian names for far-southern stars, with their true identities unknown to the more northern Arabs, while others of them were surely the creations of pre-Islamic Arabian poets.

starNames.name: Nahn
starNames.origin: "Nahn", the Persian term for "Nose", given to ξ Cnc in the NASA Memorandum by Rhoads (1971).

starNames.name: Miaplacidus
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times, and of unknown astronomical significance. The first element, Mia-, is unexplained. The second element is the Latin adjective placidus, meaning "calm, gentle" (here in the masculine form).

starNames.name: Aspidiske
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Greek word ἀσπιδίσκη, "little shield", used by Ptolemy in the Almagest in describing several stars in his constellation Argo, that were fixed to the ship for protection and decoration. Ptolemy's shields were in today's Puppis and Vela, but their identification was confused when Argo was divided into the modern Carina, Puppis, and Vela.

starNames.name: Markeb
starNames.origin: Evidently from the Arabic word markab, "a ship or any vehicle," presumably standing for the Greek constellation name Argo. However, Arabic sources do not mention markab for Argo, only al-safina ("the Ship"), hence the ultimate origin of the name remains a mystery. "Markeb" was applied as a star name to ρ Pup in medieval times, to κ Pup in Early Modern rimes, and finally to κ Vel in recent times when Argo was divided into its four modern constellations

starNames.name: Alphard
starNames.origin: Applied in medieval times from its pre-Islamic Arabian name al-fard, "the Solitary One," descriptive of this star's standing out among the surrounding dim stars. (See the same word in the plural, with ζ CMa.)

starNames.name: Intercrus
starNames.origin: Intercrus means "between the legs" in Latin style, referring to the star's position in the constellation Ursa Major.

starNames.name: Alterf
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the pre-Islamic Arabian lunar mansion name al-tarf, "the Glance," for κ Cnc and λ Leo, associated with the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism al-asad, as if being located on that lion's eyes.

starNames.name: Ukdah
starNames.origin: Kazwini knew the stars tau1, tau2 Hya as عقدة ʽuqdah (or ʽuḳdah), Arabic "knot". Rhoads (1971) considers this asterism consisting of four stars: tau1, tau2, 33 and ι Hya.

starNames.name: Subra
starNames.origin: From the pre-Islamic Arabian lunar mansion name al-zubra, "the Mane, or Shoulder," for δ and θ Leo, associated with the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism al-asad (see ε Gem; al-zubra was an alternative name for al-kharatan given under θ Leo). "Subra" was wrongly applied as a star name too Leo in recent times.

starNames.name: Zhang
starNames.origin: determinitive star of lunar mansion Zhang (The Stomach [of the Red Fire Bird] or a Bow or Bird Catcher, an Extended Net, Spread or "to open") whose naming constellation constists of 6 stars according to sources back to the 3rd millennium BCE

starNames.name: Rasalas
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of its name for the Arabic Almagest period ra's alasad (al-shamali), "(the Northern [Part] of) the Lion's Head." As originally applied, μ Leo was "Rasalasad Borealis" abbreviated in the first Western astronomical source as "Rasalas. Bor.," for lack of space in the line), and ε Leo was "Rasalasad Australis" (after the Arabic).

starNames.name: Felis
starNames.origin: Felis (The Cat) is the name of a constellation invented by Lalande. The name is applied to one star in the area that the constellation covered.

starNames.name: Yunü
starNames.origin: Yunü御女 is the star in the middle of the southernmost stars of the Xuanyuan轩辕 constellation. The correct transliteration is "Yunü".

starNames.name: Regulus
starNames.origin: The name is a Latin translation of the ancient Greek name for this star: βασιλίσκος, "the (little) King" or "the Kingly One", which is a translation of the Sumerian name of the star: LUGAL (The King). The Romans, following the Greeks, called the star stella regia, "the Royal Star". Later, the Medieval Latin Almagest, translating from the Arabic (where in one version the original Greek diminutive had been lost), had rex, "the King". The form "Regulus" (again, the [little] King") first appears in 1522, obviously formed by some Early Modern scholar after the Greek diminutive name.

starNames.name: Adhafera
starNames.origin: From the name for the Arabic Almagest period al-dafira, "the Lock of Hair," for the Coma Berenices cluster. Wrongly applied to zeta Leonis in recent times. Yet, misapplications of terms for the "hairy" cluster that is called "Coma" to the mane of the lion can be traced back to (at least) the 17th century.

starNames.name: Tania Borealis
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from their pre-Islamic Arabian name al-qafza al-thaniya, "the Second Leap", and the Latin distinctions of "northern" and "southern," respectively.

starNames.name: Algieba
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the pre-Islamic Arabian lunar mansion name al-jabha "the Forehead," for ζ, γ, η, and α Leo, associated with the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism al-asad.

starNames.name: Tania Australis
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from their pre-Islamic Arabian name al-qafza al-thaniya, "the Second Leap", and the Latin distinctions of "northern" and "southern," respectively.

starNames.name: Shaomin
starNames.origin: Taimin太民 (or Damin大民) for o Leo and Shaomin少民 (ρ Leo) are the two southernmost stars of the Xuanyuan轩辕 constellation. They were used to star names in ancient China.

starNames.name: Praecipua
starNames.origin: Piazzi (1814) in his star catalogue introduced this proper name for the star because Hevelius (1690) had added the adjective "praecipua" (Chief) as a description of this star.

starNames.name: Chalawan
starNames.origin: Chalawan is a mythological crocodile king from a Thai folktale.

starNames.name: Alkes
starNames.origin: Applied with various spellings since medieval times, from the Arabic constellation name al-ka's, "the (Wine) Cup," for Crater.

starNames.name: Merak
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of its name for the Arabic Almagest period maraqq al-dubb al-akbar, "the Flank (or Groin) of the Greater Bear."

starNames.name: Dubhe
starNames.origin: Applied in medieval times from the Arabic constellation name al-dubb, "the Bear," for Ursa Major. The spelling in the oldest sources was edubh (corresponding to the Arabic noun with the article al prefixed as e). Afterwards, by corruption, the initial e was transferred to the end of the word: dubhe.

starNames.name: Zosma
starNames.origin: From the Greek word ζῶσμα, "girdle" or "loin cloth". In Early Modern times this word was erroneously said to have been used to describe δ Leo in a medieval Greek text. Correctly, the text has ὀσφῦς, "hip" or "lower back" (after Ptolemy). The name "Zosma" (transliterated from the erroneous Greek word) was applied in recent times.

starNames.name: Chertan
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from one spelling of the pre-Islamic Arabian lunar mansion name al-khurtan, "the Two Small Ribs (at or near the breast)," for δ and θ Leo. The more common and apparently correct spelling of the lunar mansion name is al-kharatan, of unknown meaning.

starNames.name: Alula Australis
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from their pre-Islamic Arabian name al-qafza al-ula, "the First Leap", and the Latin distinctions of "northern" and "southern," respectively.

starNames.name: Alula Borealis
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from their pre-Islamic Arabian name al-qafza al-ula, "the First Leap", and the Latin distinctions of "northern" and "southern," respectively.

starNames.name: Giausar
starNames.origin: From the Persian word jauzahr, a technical term designating the nodes of the moon's or any planet's orbit. Erroneously applied as a star name to λ Dra in recent times.

starNames.name: Formosa
starNames.origin: Formosa is the historical name of Taiwan used in the 17th century, meaning beautiful in Latin.

starNames.name: Taiyangshou
starNames.origin: traditional Chinese single star asterism: Taiyangshou means "The Guardian of the Great Yang" and is the general in charge of the yang valve, symbolising Chief Minister. Xu, Pankenier and Jiang (2000) and Sun Shuwei (Stellarium) evaluating the medieval Song map, both identify chi UMa but Sun and Kistemaker (1997) studying the Han dynasty identify psi UMa.

starNames.name: Denebola
starNames.origin: Applied with various spellings since medieval times, from its name for the Arabic Almagest period dhanab al-asad, "the Lion's Tail."

starNames.name: Zavijava
starNames.origin: From a contraction of the pre-Islamic Arabian name zawiyat al-'awwa', "the Angle of al-'awwa'," for γ Vir. Wrongly transferred to β Vir in recent times. The stars β, η, γ, and ε Vir marked the pre-Islamic Arabian lunar mansion al-'awwa' (with γ in its "angle"), but the meaning of al-'awwa' is unknown.

starNames.name: Phecda
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of its name for the Arabic Almagest period fakhidh al-dubb al-akbar, "the Thigh of the Greater Bear."

starNames.name: Tonatiuh
starNames.origin: Tonatiuh was the Aztec god of the Sun.

starNames.name: Alchiba
starNames.origin: From the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism name al-khibāʾ, “the Tent,” for β, γ, δ and ε Crv. Wrongly applied as a star name to α Crv in recent times.

starNames.name: Imai
starNames.origin: The Mursi name a line of four stars imai (δ Cru), thaadoi (β Cru), waar (β Cen) and sholbi (α Cen). Their successive disappearance (heliacal setting) are used to determine when the River Omo will flood (it does this several times) and hence to determine when to plant the annual crop of cowpeas beside it (after the last flood but before the ground dries out). Imai is the Mursi name for the grass that grows along the banks of the river (Rhynchelytrum repens). It is said that when the imai star disappears, the Omo rises high enough to flatten the imai grass.

starNames.name: Megrez
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of its name for the Arabic Almagest period maghriz al-dubb al-akbar, "the Root (of the tail) of the Greater Bear."

starNames.name: Gienah
starNames.origin: A name transferred from γ Crv in recent times, where the Arabic word janab means "wing" (in the Almagest, both ε Cyg and γ Crv lie on the wings of their respective constellations)

starNames.name: Zaniah
starNames.origin: From an abbreviation of the pre-Islamic Arabian name zawiyat al-'awwa', "the Angle of al-'awwa'," for γ Vir. Wrongly transferred to η Vir in recent times.

starNames.name: Ginan
starNames.origin: Ginan is the Wardaman name of ε Cru, from the Northern Territory, Australia. Ginan was found by Mulugurnden (the crayfish), who brought the red flying foxes from the underworld to the sky. The bats flew up the track of the Milky Way and traded the spiritual song with Guyaru, the Night Owl (Sirius). The bats fly through the constellation Scorpius on their way to the Southern Cross, trading songs as they go. The song informs the people about initiation, which is managed by the stars in Scorpius and related to Larawag (who ensures the appropriate personnel are present for the final stages of the ceremony). The colour of the star is reflected as the brownish-red colour of the dilly bag and its association with ceremonial fire.

starNames.name: Acrux
starNames.origin: A modern creation (1938) that is derived from Bayer's nomenclature by combining the "A" from the "alpha" in α Crucis and the Latin constellation name in the nominative case.

starNames.name: Algorab
starNames.origin: From an abbreviation of the name for the Arabic Almagest period janab al-ghurab, "the Raven's Wing," for γ Crv. Transferred to δ Crv in Early Modern times (both γ and δ were on the Raven's wings in the Almagest).

starNames.name: Gacrux
starNames.origin: Contraction of Gamma and Crux, appearing in the 1940s.

starNames.name: Chara
starNames.origin: Applied in Early Modern times from the Greek word χαρά, "joy", that was used by Hevelius in 1690 to name the southern dog (marked by α and β CVn) in his new constellation Canes Vanatici.

starNames.name: Kraz
starNames.origin: Name of unknown etymology from the "Atlas Coeli Skalnaté Pleso" of Czech astronomer Antonín Bečvář (1901-1965).

starNames.name: Phyllon Kissinou
starNames.origin: Contemporary modern astronomers have used the nickname "Kissin"; therefore, the real name was made official. The term originates from the phrase "φύλλοv κισσίνου (phyllon kissinou, an ivy leaf)" in Ptolemy's Almagest. The star might be "multiple or double" according to SIMBAD, so long double name for the visible dot in the sky might be split up to the components later.

starNames.name: Porrima
starNames.origin: The name of a Roman goddess, one of several mythological names mentioned in connection with the constellation Virgo. Applied as a star name in recent times.

starNames.name: Lumbung
starNames.origin: The term "Lumbung" is inherited from Malay, Proto-Malayo-Polynesian, designating a quickly set up rice barn or granary. The constellation of Lumbung is attested for ~1300 years in the cultural calendar and associated with Wednesday and the third day of an Oceanic market cycle.

starNames.name: La Superba
starNames.origin: In 1868 Secchi used "superba" as an adjective to describe the star Y CVn, not as a proper name of the star. However, in 1876 Birmingham seems to have borrowed from Secchi this term and used it as a proper name of the star. As a consequence, in 1877 Secchi himself adopted the same name. Agnes Clerke attributed the term to Secchi, without distinguishing between the adjective and the name. In principle, it should be attributed to both Secchi and Birmingham, in my opinion.

starNames.name: Tianyi
starNames.origin: Chinese single star asterism: heavenly unity

starNames.name: Mimosa
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times, and of unknown astronomical significance. It is from the Latin word mimus, "an actor", and is otherwise known as the genus name for certain tropical plants.

starNames.name: Alioth
starNames.origin: Ultimately from its pre-Islamic Arabian name al-jaun, "the Black Horse, or Bull," which became corrupted even in Arabic sources (where some of the corruptions carried other meanings). For example, in the Arabic manuscript of the Almagest that was translated into Latin in 1175 A.D., this name of ε UMa had apparently been miswritten as al-jauza or al-jauza (the latter being identical to the name for the Arabic Almagest period for Orion and Gemini). Whatever was read in this Arabic manuscript was transliterated into Latin as alioze. In subsequent Latin copies, this name was further corrupted to aliore, Alcor, Alioth, etc. Since late medieval times, "Alioth" became the preferred name for ε UMa.

starNames.name: Taiyi
starNames.origin: single star asterism: August Unity, Supreme One

starNames.name: Minelauva
starNames.origin: The 13th Arabic lunar station bears the name العوا) Al-ʿAwwā, The bend. It consists of 5 stars: β, η, γ, δ and ε Vir. "Auva" or "Minelauva" are mediaeval transliterations of this name that now names one of its stars.

starNames.name: Cor Caroli
starNames.origin: The name first appeared in 1673 on the northern half of a pair of celestial hemispheres that accompanied a book called Astroscopium by the English cartographer Francis Lamb. He labelled the star Cor Caroli Regis Martyris, a reference to the fact that King Charles I was beheaded, or ‘martyred’, as Lamb loyally put it (Charles had declared himself ‘martyr of the people’ at his execution).

starNames.name: Vindemiatrix
starNames.origin: The formation of this name begins with the classical Greek name for this star: Protrygeter ("the Grape Gatherer") as it is given in the Almagest: ὁ βόρειος αὐτῶv καὶ καλούμενος Προτρυγητήρ. The Romans translated this name as vindemiator and other similiar masculine forms. Similarly, after a somewhat erroneous translation of the Greek name by the Arabs, the Medieval Latin translation in the Almagest was precedens vindemiatorem, "the One preceding the Grape Gatherer", modified in some editions of the Alphonsine Tables into precedens vindemitorem. The exact origin of the current, feminine "Vindemiatrix" from any of these forms is uncertain, but it first appeared in Early Modern times.

starNames.name: Naga
starNames.origin: Sanskrit नाग, nāgá, means “large snake” or "serpent". Languages like Iban, Indonesian, Italian, Javanese, Malay, Marano, Portuguese, Tagalog and Yakan borrow the term; Japanese "naga" means "long"; German "Nagel" (nail) and English "naked" are derived from homophonous Sanskrit "nāga" for gold/ iron/ metal.

starNames.name: Kulou
starNames.origin: "Kulou" (库楼) means arsenal and storied building. It is a super-constellation in the area of modern Cen/Lup created in ancient China, dating back to the 2nd century BCE.

starNames.name: Mizar
starNames.origin: Ultimately from the Arabic word al-maraqq, "the Groin," used in the Arabic Almagest in describing β UMa. Correct transliterations of almaraqq in the Medieval Latin Almagest were mirac and mirach. However, Early Modern scholars confused these words with the Arabic word mi'zar, which had equally been transliterated and corrupted in Latin as mirac, mirach, etc. Subsequently the mistaken mi'zar, written as "Mizar," was applied as a star name to β UMa, and it became transferred to ζ UMa in late Early Modern times.

starNames.name: Spica
starNames.origin: Its ancient Roman name meaning "the Ear of Grain", after the star's Greek name στάχυς of identical meaning (in turn having obvious origins among the Babylonians and Sumerians). Reapplied in Early Modern times.

starNames.name: Alcor
starNames.origin: Ultimately from the pre-Islamic Arabian name al-jaun, for ε UMa, which was transliterated and eventually corrupted in Latin to "Alcor." The name was wrongly transferred to 80 UMa in Early Modern times.

starNames.name: Apamvatsa
starNames.origin: Apāṃvatsa (अपऻऺवत्स), "calf of the waters" (or: "the smaller one"), is an Indian star name attested throughout the last millennium. The only indication of the position is Apamvatsa is 5° to the north of Citrā (चित्रा) (Spica) in Virgo, attested in several historical documents.

starNames.name: Heze
starNames.origin: Name of unknown etymology from the "Atlas Coeli Skalnaté Pleso" of Czech astronomer Antonín Bečvář (1901-1965). It could refer to God, possibly derived from Ezechiel (one of four prophets from Old Testament). Transcription to the Greek language adds "H" to EZE.

starNames.name: Jordanus
starNames.origin: Jordanus was used as a constellation name by Plancius in his 1612 celestial map, which introduced some uniting elements for Europeans fighting each other in the early modern spirit of an "under one sky"-philosophy.

starNames.name: Tepiamenit
starNames.origin: Menit, The Mooring Post, is an Egyptian constellation, preserved in Ramesside Star Clocks of the 2nd millennium BCE. Tepiamenit is the "Predecessor of the Pole" inside Menit.

starNames.name: Alkaid
starNames.origin: Applied with various spellings since medieval times, from its pre-Islamic Arabian name al-qa'id, "the Leader" (probably as leader of the Daughters of the Bier).

starNames.name: Heng
starNames.origin: Heng is an old Chinese name of a constellation within the super-constellation of Kulou, The Arsenal. The translation is not certain; probably a measuring device.

starNames.name: Muphrid
starNames.origin: The formation of this name begins with the ancient Arabic name for α Boo: al-simak al-ramih, "the Lance-bearing simak" (the meaning of simak is uncertain). It seems that later Arabic poets expanded upon this name by making mention of some separate "lance" (al-rumh) that accompanied the star α Boo. Subsequent Arabs attempted to identify this fictitious lance with actual stars, sometimes saying it was η Boo with nearby stars, sometimes saying it was "η Boo alone" (where "alone", in arabic, is written mufradan). From these discussions came, with a slight copying mistake in the Arabic, the erroneous Arabic name mufrad al-ramih, roughly translating as "the Isolated Single One of the Lance-Bearer". With a wrong vocalization and with abbreviation, this erroneous name, as "Muphrid", was applied in recent times.

starNames.name: Leepwal
starNames.origin: Ļeepwal is the name for ζ Cen in Marshallese. Original spelling Ļeepwal. Pronounced leyepwal, the first "l" being pronounced with the back of the tongue raised (velarized) and the root of the tongue retracted (pharyngealized) so as to elongate the oral cavity, thereby giving the consonant a "heavier" or "darker" sound.

starNames.name: Hadar
starNames.origin: From some pre-Islamic Arabian name hadari (an untranslated proper name), for one of a pair of stars, the other one being al-wazn. Sci-A authors ventured to identify these stars as α/β Cen or α/β Col, but exactly what two stars were originally intended, and the significance of their names, is unknown. "Hadar" was arbitrarily applied to β Cen in recent times.

starNames.name: Thuban
starNames.origin: The formation of this name begins with the name for the Arabic Almagest period for γ Dra: ra's al-tinnin, "the Serpent's Head." In medieval times this was transliterated into Latin as raztaben, rahtaben, razcaben, and several other corruptions (eventually leading to the name for β Dra). By Early Modern times the form Rastaben had appeared, and this name was erroneously attributed, in its last part, to the Arabic word thu'ban, "serpent", rather than to al-tinnin (subsequently thu<ban was wrongly regarded as a name for the Arabic Almagest period for the constellation Draco). Finally in recent times, the erroneous word, written as "Thuban," was applied as a star name to α Dra.

starNames.name: Menkent
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times and possibly coined from the Arabic word mankib, "shoulder" (in some recent transliterations: menkib; Ptolemy described this star on the right "shoulder" of the Centaur), plus the Latinized "Kentaurus" for the Arabic constellation name qanturis. Hence this name could be of similar construction to the abbreviation for α Cen: "Rigil Kent."

starNames.name: Kang
starNames.origin: determinitive star of lunar mansion Kang (The Neck) whose naming constellation constists of 4 stars according to sources back to the 3rd millennium BCE

starNames.name: Arcturus
