starNames.origin: From its ancient Greek name Ἀρκτοῦρος, "the Guard, or Guardian". Reapplied in Early Modern times. As the Greek word Άρκτος, "bear," also came to mean "north," the meaning can ambiguously be "Guardian of the North" and "Guardian of the Bear", referring to the nearby constellation Ursa Major.

starNames.name: Syrma
starNames.origin: From the Greek word σύρμα, "train of a dress", used by Ptolemy in the Almagest in describing this star. The word was applied as a star name in recent times.

starNames.name: Xuange
starNames.origin: single star asterism: a halberd, the celestial lance or north lance.

starNames.name: Khambalia
starNames.origin: The Coptic (Egyptian) term Khambalia means "Crooked-clawed" (perhaps designating an agricultural device or symbol of secret knowledge); it was used in mantic texts for the star in the foot of Virgo.

starNames.name: Elgafar
starNames.origin: This name is a rare transliteration of Arabic الغفر al-ghafr (or "El-ġafr"), The Cover. This transliteration was used by Ideler (1809) but is uncommon today except in the Arabic Maghreb (northwest Africa). It is the name of the 15th lunar station (5 Oct).

starNames.name: Kalasungsang
starNames.origin: On Bali (Indonesia) "Kala" means "demon" and "sungsang" means "upside down". Originally, the term is from Sanskrit काल, dark/ death or time. The daemon reminds us not to waste time.

starNames.name: Seginus
starNames.origin: The formation of this name begins with the Greek constellation name βοώτης (Boötes), which was transliterated and then corrupted in the manuscripts of the Arabic Almagest. One of these corruptions, in turn, was transliterated into Latin as theguius, which became further corrupted into cheguius, ceginus, etc. One form, Ceginus, was applied as a star name by late medieval times, and "Seginus" is its recent spelling.

starNames.name: Genghe
starNames.origin: Gěnghé (Celestial Lance, 梗河) is a Chinese constellation of 3 stars. WGSN named the second star in the line.

starNames.name: Toliman
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from some pre-Islamic Arabian name al-zulman, "the Ostriches." Stars in today's Centaurus were variously identified with one or more ostriches by the pre-Islamic Arabians, but what star or stars were originally designated is unknown.

starNames.name: Rigil Kentaurus
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from its name for the Arabic Almagest period rijl qanturis, "the Centaur's Foot". Today the name is occasionally seen abbreviated as "Rigil Kent."

starNames.name: Uridim
starNames.origin: The constellation of Lupus is one of the few ancient "Greek" constellation outside the zodiac that was directly taken over from a Babylonian constellation. The Sumerian term for this creature was UR.IDIM, later alternatively written "Uridimmu" in the Akkadian language (the literal Akkadian translation of UR.IDIM would be "kalbu šegû", according to lexical lists).

starNames.name: Xami
starNames.origin: The South African asterism "Eyes of the Lion" refers to alpha and beta Centauri. Assuming these bright stars are the eyes, the face of this creature "Xami" covers alf Cir, and the constellation Circinus does not have any mythology or alternative name. Therefore, WGSN decided for an Indigenous name for this main star of a constellation.

starNames.name: Alrumh
starNames.origin: Al-Rumḥ (الرُّمْح), the Lance/ Spear, is an Arabic asterism from pre-Islamic times that covers the area between Epsilon, Upsilon, Eta and Sigma Bootis. The named star is close to the dominant Epsilon Bootis, which also forms part of the Chinese constellation of The Lance (Genghe).

starNames.name: Izar
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Arabic word izwar, "girdle" or "loin cloth", being a later version of the original term al-mi)zar used in the Arabic Almagest in describing this star.

starNames.name: Pulcherrima
starNames.origin: The Latin name translates to "most beautiful" or "loveliest," referring to its striking, contrasting colors; it was introduced by F. Struve in 1837.

starNames.name: Maenalus
starNames.origin: Mons Maenalus is an early modern European constellation or asterism introduced by Hevelius (1690), setting a celestial memorial for a mountain in the central Peloponnese, Greece.

starNames.name: Paradys
starNames.origin: In Dutch around 1600, two spelling versions of the Apus-bird existed. WGSN decided to take the first part of the earliest written witness, Paradys-vogel (Plancius 1598), to name the main star of the constellation.

starNames.name: Merga
starNames.origin: A Latin word meaning "reaping hook," used in a Early Modern discussion of the constellation Bootes. According to this discussion, some classical sources mentioned a reaping hook held in Bootes' hand opposite the staff. Subsequently the word was applied as a star name to hBoo.

starNames.name: Solitaire
starNames.origin: extinct constellations invented by Le Monnier (1776), Latinized "Turdus Solitarius", was originally meant to remember the extinct bird "Rodrigues Solitaire", but always depicted as a Blue Rock Thrush.

starNames.name: Kochab
starNames.origin: Applied to β UMi in Early Modern times and of uncertam derivation. It is probably from one of the names Alrucaba, Rucaba, etc., that were first applied to θ UMa, then to α UMi, in medieval times. However, the name may also be from the Arabic word kaukab, or the Hebrew word kokhabh, both meaning "star."

starNames.name: Zubenelgenubi
starNames.origin: Applied in Early Modern times from its name for the Arabic Almagest period al-zubana al-janubi, the Southern Claw ( of the Scorpion)." The stars of Libra were interpreted by the Baby!onians as "the Claws of Scorpius" (thus forming a much larger Scorpion), and alternatively (perhaps in a more recent stage) they were made an independent constellation, "the Balance." Both these conceptions lived on until the Greeks and, partly, the pre-Islamic Arabians. Previous to Greek influences, the pre-Islamic Arabians used the name al-zubanayan, "the Two Claws ( of the Scorpion}," for the lunar mansion marked by α and β Lib. (Ind-A al-zubanayan is obviously related etymologically to Babylonian zibanutu, but the latter, also marked by α and β Lib, meant "the Balance"). Our modern name is occasionally seen abbreviated as Zuben'ubi".

starNames.name: Nekkar
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from a misreading of the Arabic constellation name al-baqqar, "the Ox-driver", for Boötes.

starNames.name: Quadrans
starNames.origin: Quadrans Muralis is an obsolete constellation invented in 1795 by the French astronomer Jérôme Lalande. WGSN decided to commemorate this constellation as it is the root of the name of the Quadrantide meteor shower that peaks in the first days of January.

starNames.name: Brachium
starNames.origin: For Bayer (1603), this star is γ Scorpii with no proper name but in the register for the Scorpius-star chart, he lists "Virgilius brachium" among other (Greek and Arabic) designations for this star. Allen (1899, 368/9) that Vergil had not meant it as a star name but only as a marker for the "claws", so it was never meant as a proper name.

starNames.name: Qigong
starNames.origin: Qī Gōng (Seven Excellencies, 七公) is a Chinese asterism composed of seven stars; WGSN named the determinative star after the constellation.

starNames.name: Zubeneschamali
starNames.origin: Applied in Early Modern times from its name for the Arabic Almagest period al-zubana alshamali, "the Northern Claw (of the Scorpion)".

starNames.name: Pherkad Minor
starNames.origin: One of Piazzi's star names following the schema of naming a faint visual neighbour in reference to the visually more striking star in a constellation.

starNames.name: Pherkad
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the singular form of the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism name al-farqadan, "the Two Calves," for β and γ UMi.

starNames.name: Alkalurops
starNames.origin: The formation of this name begins with one of the words used by Ptolemy to describe this star in the Almagest: κολλόροβον, "club", rarely used as "sphepherd's staff". This word was transliterated into Arabic as qulurubus, and hence into Latin as calurus. Then in Early Modern times, the derivation of calurus was mistakenly attributed to another Greek word: καλαῦροψ, "shepherd's staff". This erroneous word, in its turn, was transliterated into Latin, then Arabicized with the article al-, then its spelling corrupted, to become "Alkalurops", which was thereafter applied as a star name to μ Boo.

starNames.name: Edasich
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from its pre-Islamic Arabian name al-dhikh, "the Male Hyena."

starNames.name: Nusakan
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the collective pre-Islamic Arabian name al-nasaqan, "the Two Lines [of stars]" for two asterisms in today's Hercules, Serpens, Ophiuchus, and Lyra. al-nasaqan originally marked the boundaries of the pre-Islamic Arabian 'al-rauda, "the Pasture". These boundaries were "the Northern Line" al-nasaq al-sha'ami, and "the Southern Line" al-nasaq al-yamani.

starNames.name: Guansuo
starNames.origin: Guàn Suǒ (Coiled Thong, 贯索), a Chinese constellation of 9 stars in CrB. It resembles a string threaded through a series of copper coins, attested since ancient times.

starNames.name: Alphecca
starNames.origin: Applied in medieval times from the pre-Islamic Arabian asterism name al-fakka, for Corona Borealis. The Arabic name, from the root f-k-k, "to separate, break up, etc.," apparently refers to this asterism's shape: an incomplete circle.

starNames.name: Zubenelhakrabi
starNames.origin: Allen (1899) claims that this term was used for η Lib while “properly belonging to γ Scorpii”. He gives the name “Zubān alʿAkrab, the Scropion’s Claw,” with the spelling variants Zuban al Kravi, Zuben Acrabi, Zuben Hakrabi where the last one goes back to Bayer’s Uranometria (1603). Yet, Bayer’s γ Scorpii is now σ Lib (Brachium) and Bayer’s γ Lib was named “in media lance Boreali prima et superior”.

starNames.name: Baltesha
starNames.origin: (MUL.)BAL.TEŠ2.A (𒀯𒁄𒌨𒀀), the Asterism of Dignity, is an ancient Sumerian constellation in CrB.

starNames.name: Stephanos
starNames.origin: Στέφανος, The Wreath, is the ancient Greek name of CrB. It can represent either the laurel wreath of an emperor or victorious athlete, or a bridal wreath.

starNames.name: Unukalhai
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from its name for the Arabic Almagest period 'unuq al-hayya, "the Serpent's Neck."

starNames.name: Zhou
starNames.origin: This is a traditional Chinese star name of one of the stars in the historical Chinese constellation of Tianshi (Celestial Marketplace).

starNames.name: Gudja
starNames.origin: Gudja is the Wardaman name of κ Ser, from the Northern Territory, Australia. Gudja is a Water Goanna, related to birth and rebirth. It is part of the bright trio of stars in Serpens Caput, which also include Munin the Rock Cod (γ Ser) and the Mungamungga birthing place (β Ser), likened to a little hospital. Gudja is involved with the birthing process, which includes sacred ritual practices. The Spiritual Women at the birthing and blessing site in Serpens Caput are connected to the sacred areas of Crux and enacted at Munin Rock and Yinggalarri.

starNames.name: Matrichakra
starNames.origin: Mātrīcakra, The Circle (मातृचक्र), is an Indian name for CrB; the Sanskrit term occurs on historical globes and astrolabes.

starNames.name: Muning
starNames.origin: Muning, "the Small Rock Cod," is a name for two stars (γ and β Ser) in Serpens from the Australian Wardaman people whose Elders approved the name for γ Ser.

starNames.name: Iklil
starNames.origin: the name derives from the Arabic lunar mansion "Iklil" (Arabic: الإكليل), "The ornamented headband" (or: diadem) composed of the 3 stars β1, δ and π Sco; here misapplied to ρ Sco.

starNames.name: Fang
starNames.origin: determinitive star of lunar mansion Fang (The Room) whose naming constellation constists of 4 stars according to sources back to the 3rd millennium BCE.

starNames.name: Dschubba
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of the name for the Arabic Almagest period jabhat al-'aqrab, "the Scorpion's Forehead," for β, δ, and π Sco.

starNames.name: Aurwandilsta
starNames.origin: Aurvandils tá, Aurvandill's Toe, is a Norse constellation from Iceland, documented in Snorri's Edda from the 13th century CE.

starNames.name: Acrab
starNames.origin: Arabic name al-'Aqrab for the constellation Scorpius ("the scorpion") (e.g. Al Sufi). Application of the transliteration "Acrab" specifically to the pair Beta1 and Beta2 Sco was made by Piazzi (1814) in the Palermo Catalog, and its use spread through the 19th century.

starNames.name: Marsic
starNames.origin: Applied in medieval times from the Arabic word al-marfiq, "the elbow," used in the Arabic Almagest in describing this star.

starNames.name: Jabbah
starNames.origin: the name was considered popular by WGSN as mentioned in Allen (1899): "in the Century Cyclopaedia, perhaps from its being one of the mansil Iklil al Jabbah."

starNames.name: Yed Prior
starNames.origin: Originally from the Arabic word al-yad, "the hand," used in the Arabic Almagest in describing these stars. yed was applied as a star name to δ Oph in medieval times. Then in recent times, this application was extended to include both δ and ε, with the addition of the Latin distinctions for "foremost" and "hindmost," respectively.

starNames.name: Yed Posterior
starNames.origin: Originally from the Arabic word al-yad, "the hand," used in the Arabic Almagest in describing these stars. yed was applied as a star name to δ Oph in medieval times. Then in recent times, this application was extended to include both δ and ε, with the addition of the Latin distinctions for "foremost" and "hindmost," respectively.

starNames.name: Asuusiha
starNames.origin: Asu Usiha (Manchu: ᠠᠰᡠ ᡠᠰᡳᡥᠠ, Net Stars), a Manchu shamanic constellation. It represents a hunting net to capture sables.

starNames.name: Alniyat
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the pre-Islamic Arabian name al-niyat, "the Arteries", for σ and τ Sco. α Sco, between the arteries, was the pre-Islamic Arabian qalb al'aqrab, "the Scorpion's Heart" (all were part of the pre-Islamic Arabian Scorpion).

starNames.name: Athebyne
starNames.origin: The transliteration Athebyne is one of several renderings of the Arabic asterism name الذئبين al-dhiʼbayn, "the (two) wolves" (ζ and η Draconis) aiming at the Camel's Foal (group of northern asterisms).

starNames.name: Cujam
starNames.origin: From the Latin word caiam, "club" (in the accusative case, nominative case "caia"), see Kunitzsch and Smart (2006). The Greek term for "club" is already a star name in Eratosthenes (Pamias and Zucker 2013).

starNames.name: Yaqana
starNames.origin: Yaqana is a mother llama and forms a super-constellation with Uñallamacha, the baby llama. They rise in the sky when baby llamas are born on Earth.

starNames.name: Antares
starNames.origin: From its ancient Greek name ἀντάρης, "like Ares", likening the red colour of this star to its planetary namesake (the Roman Mars), name occurs in the Almagest. Possibly the Greek name goes back to a Sumerian precursor AN.TA.GUB (as suggested by Horowitz).

starNames.name: Kornephoros
starNames.origin: From the Greek word κορυνηφόρος, "club-bearer", mentioned in one Early Modern study as a name for the constellation Hercules. Properly it is of mythological rather than astronomical significance, for Ptolemy's constellation here was "the Kneeler", described without a club. "Kornephoros" was applied as a star name in recent times.

starNames.name: Marfik
starNames.origin: Applied since medieval times from the Arabic word al-marfiq, "the elbow," used in the Arabic Almagest in describing this star. While the medieval transliteration was marsic (with a confusion of f and the long-shaped s), Marfik is an improved spelling of recent times.

starNames.name: Paikauhale
starNames.origin: Au-haele, Hōkū-‘ula and Paikauhale are documented as three stars in a line, running from north to south. Two of the most reliable sources—Mary Puku‘i and Rubellite Johnson—both identify Hōkū-‘ula as Antares (α Sco), which makes Au-haele Alniyat (σ Sco) and Paikauhale τ Sco.

starNames.name: Tianji
starNames.origin: Celestial Discipline, 天紀, is an ancient Chinese asterism of nine stars first recorded in the Western Han Shishi xingjing (Master Shi’s Star Canon, 石氏星經).

starNames.name: Atria
starNames.origin: Contraction of Bayer designation A(lpha) Tri(anguli) A(ustralis). The name is listed as "Alpha Tri. Aust." in 1951 American Nautical Almanac, but listed as "Atria" in 1952 version and subsequent versions.

starNames.name: Larawag
starNames.origin: Larawag is the Wardaman name of ε Sco, from the Northern Territory, Australia. Larawag is part of a procession of beings along the curve of stars in Scorpius, acting as the signal watcher, noting when only legitimate participants are present and in view of the ceremony. He gives the “All clear” signal, allowing the secret part of the ceremony to continue. This procession is related to the bats that carry Ginan.

starNames.name: Xamidimura
starNames.origin: Originally spelled as three word "xami di mura" means "eyes of the beast" in the Khoekhoe language (South Africa). The term designates two stars which is why it was suggested (Hahn 1881) to refer to μ Sco as this star appears as a visual pair of two dots of light. Yet, today's identification popularized by the SAAO differs.

starNames.name: Pipirima
starNames.origin: There are many versions of a widespread Polynesian story of two children fleeing their uncaring parents to become two shining stars, the stars themselves being variously recorded as Castor and Pollux (α and β Gem), Shaula and Lesath (λ and υ Sco), ζ and θ Sco, and µ¹ and µ² Sco as well as [possibly] ω¹ and ω² Sco. In Tahiti, Pipiri was the twin brother of Rehua: Pipiri ma refers to the two together, ma "with, and" being used after names to mean "et al.". Calderon identifies the two children as µ¹ and µ² Sco, their mother being Shaula (λ Sco) and their father Lesath (υ Sco).

starNames.name: Shengong
starNames.origin: Shengong (神宫, Divine Palace) is a subsidiary asterism attached to the lodge Wěi (尾), Tail [of the Azure Dragon], located to the left of its determinative star and consisting of only one star (single star-asterism).

starNames.name: Khepdenreret
starNames.origin: Khepdenreret, the Buttocks of the Hippopotamus (goddess) Reret, is a star name from ancient Egypt documented in the Ramesside Star Clocks from around 1200 BCE

starNames.name: Alrakis
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from its pre-Islamic Arabian name al-raqis, "the Trotting Camel."

starNames.name: Aldhibah
starNames.origin: ζ and η Draconis together had been considered the asterism of الذئب, al-dhiʼb, Two Hyenas or Two Wolfs that are lurking for the Camel's Foal that is protected by its mother (other stars in Draco).

starNames.name: Sabik
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from its pre-Islamic Arabian name al-sabiq, of uncertain meaning or connection. The name might mean literally "the Preceding One" or "the One Arriving First in a Race". Other sources give the name in the dualis form (for the two stars ζ and η Oph), and in the plural form (for more than two stars).

starNames.name: Rasalgethi
starNames.origin: Applied with various spellings since medieval times, from its name for the Arabic Almagest period ra's al-jathi, "the Kneeler's Head."

starNames.name: Sarin
starNames.origin: Name of unknown etymology from the "Atlas Coeli Skalnaté Pleso" of Czech astronomer Antonín Bečvář (1901-1965). It is probably a part of the body. The word probably is not of Semit's origin,

starNames.name: Nüchuang
starNames.origin: Nǚ Chuáng (Women’s Bed, 女床) is a small asterism consisting of only three stars that dates back to around 100 BCE and belongs to the Shi school.

starNames.name: Guniibuu
starNames.origin: Guniibuu is the Kamilaroi/Euahlayi name for the robin red-breast bird (Petroica boodang). A traditional story links Guniibuu with Gidjirrigaa (Budgerigar) the star κ Sco.

starNames.name: Uñallamacha
starNames.origin: Uñallamacha, The Baby Llama, is an Inka dark constellation. It forms a super-constellation with its mother, Yaqana. WGSN picked the faintest star above the visibility threshold and inside the dark cloud area to keep its heritage.

starNames.name: Rastaban
starNames.origin: Applied with various spellings since medieval times, from the name for the Arabic Almagest period ra's al-tinnin, "the Serpent's Head," for γ Dra. Transferred to β Dra in recent times (originally Ptolemy had γ Dra on the "head," and β more specifically on the "eye").

starNames.name: Maasym
starNames.origin: From the Arabic word al-mi'sam, "the wrist," used in the Arabic Almagest in describing o Her. Wrongly transferred to λ Her in Early Modern times.

starNames.name: Lesath
starNames.origin: The formation of this name begins with the Greek term "(foggy) conglomeration," used by Ptolemy in the Tetrabiblos in describing several nebulous sky objects (in the present case, probably the open cluster M7). Ptolemy's term was translated by the Arabs as al-latkha, "the Spot." This word in turn became transliterated and corrupted in Medieval Latin to alascha, which was used in astrological texts in connection with Scorpius' tail. In Early Modern times, the derivation of alascha was erroneously attributed to the Arabic word las'a, "sting, or bite (of a poisonous animal)," rather than to al-latkha. Subsequently the erroneous word, written as "Lesath," was applied as a star name to u Sco (and in recent times, also to λ Sco).

starNames.name: Yildun
starNames.origin: From the Turkish word yildiz, "star." In Early Modern times this common noun was erroneously said to be a Turkish name for the Pole Star (α UMi). Misspelled as "Yildun," the word was arbitrarily applied as a star name to δ UMi in recent times.

starNames.name: Alawaidh
starNames.origin: al-ʿAwāʾidh (العَوائِذ), The Camel Mothers, derives from an Arabic asterism: four camel mothers are protecting one newborn camel calf (Alruba, HIP 86782).

starNames.name: Shaula
starNames.origin: The Arabic lunar mansion "Al Shaula" ("the sting") refers to the pair Lambda and Upsilon Sco (Al Sufi), the two stars that have been called "the sting of the Scorpion" even in MUL.APIN (I ii 31-32) but with different proper names there. "Shaula" appeared more in early modern literature for the pair of stinger stars after Hyde's (1665) translation of Ulugh Beg, and specifically for Lambda Sco after Piazzi's (1814) Palermo Catalog.

starNames.name: Rasalhague
starNames.origin: Applied with various spellings since medieval times, from its name for the Arabic Almagest period ra's al-ḥawwa', "the Head of the Serpent Collector."

starNames.name: Sargas
starNames.origin: MUL.SHAR.GAZ, "mul" is the Sumerian designator for stars and constellations, "Shargaz" and "Sharur" are two weapons of Marduk (the city god of Babylon and highest god of the Babylonian pantheon after 1250 BCE). The line I ii 31-32 in MUL.APIN read: "Two stars which stand in the sting of the Scorpion: Sharur and Shargaz", so these star names have originally been given to the stars lambda and upsilon Sco. The Mesopotamian name "Sargas" was linked to the star Theta Sco by Robert Brown Jr. (1893; "Euphratean Stellar Researches Part II.") and its subsequent mention in R. H. Allen's (1899) "Star-names and Their Meanings" popularized its subsequent use.

starNames.name: Tianbang
starNames.origin: Tiān Bàng (Celestial Flail, 天棓) is a defensive weapon, attested as constellation since 100 BCE. WGSN represents it by its determinative star.

starNames.name: Dziban
starNames.origin: Dsiban, from Al Dhibain (the Arabs' title for ζ and η), has been given by some to this pair [ψ1, ψ2 Dra].

starNames.name: Cebalrai
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from its pre-Islamic Arabian name kalb al-ra'i, "the Shepherd's Dog" (in other traditions α Her and 28/29 Cep are given the same name). This dog, together with the shepherd (marked by α Oph), and the two lines of stars enclosing the Pasture, and all the dim stellar sheep in that portion of the sky (al-ghanam or al-aghnam for the sheep), seem to form a complete group of pre-Islamic Arabian figures.

starNames.name: Alruba
starNames.origin: Arabic الربع Al Rubaʽ translates "the foal" and specifically refers to a young camel born in the spring. The name was considered traditional by WGSN in 2018 as it is listed in Allen (1899).

starNames.name: Cervantes
starNames.origin: Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra (1547-1616) was a famous Spanish writer and author of "El Ingenioso Hidalgo Don Quixote de la Mancha".

starNames.name: Bake-eo
starNames.origin: A Marshallese star name for γ Oph. Pronounced "bakey-yew". Both spellings, "Bake-eo" and "Bake Eo" are accepted. The particle "Eo" simply means "here it is, take it", Bake is the spondylus mussel.

starNames.name: Fuyue
starNames.origin: traditional Chinese single star asterism: a legendary wise minister of the Yin or Shang dynasty, 18th century BCE. According to Rufus and Tien (1945), sometimes called the invocator (regarding faults). Sun and Kistemaker (1997) quote Sima Qian that Fu Yue was a chancellor of Emperor Wu Ding of the Yin dynasty but they admit that the could also represent a shaman in the royal harem helping to produce sons. The ancient star name is typically identified with the bright star G Sco.

starNames.name: Grumium
starNames.origin: A Late Latin word (its correct spelling should be grunnum) meaning "snout" or "muzzle (especially of a pig)", used in the Medieval Latin Almagest in describing this star. The word was applied as a star name in recent times.

starNames.name: Eltanin
starNames.origin: Applied in Early Modern times from the Arabic constellation name al-tinnīn, “the serpent”, for Draco.

starNames.name: Tianyue
starNames.origin: Tiān Yuè (天籥, Celestial Keyhole) is a Chinese constellation believed to govern the functions of opening and closing.

starNames.name: Bodu
starNames.origin: Bó Dù (帛度, “Textile Ruler”) is a Chinese asterism consisting of two stars, established by the Wuxian (巫咸) tradition during the Han dynasty. WGSN chose to adopt the name according to the Yi Shitong catalog because earlier identifications are highly uncertain.

starNames.name: Dhanuśarāgra
starNames.origin: Dhanuśarāgra (धनुशराग्र), The Arrow, is an Indian star name found on astrolabes since the 14th century CE for a star in (Greek) Sagittarius.

starNames.name: Alnasl
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from its late Arabic name al-nasl, "the Point," in turn an abbreviation of the Arabic Almagest's nasl al-sahm, "the Point of the Arrow."

starNames.name: Ramus
starNames.origin: Ramus, The Branch (of golden apples), is an addition to the early modern asterism Cerberus in Hercules. The name occurs in Bayer (1603) as a term but in depiction only later.

starNames.name: Polis
starNames.origin: the term in Coptic means "a foal." It was originally used for stars in the bow of the Archer but was moved over time.

starNames.name: Heryibwia
starNames.origin: Wia, The Boat, is a large ancient Egyptian constellation in Sco & Sgr; “Heryib Wia”, The Middle of the Boat, is a star mentioned in the diagonal star clocks, c. 2300 BCE.

starNames.name: Kaus Media
starNames.origin: Arbitrarily applied in recent times, together with the Latin distinctions of "middle," "southern," and "northern" (for λ Sgr), from the pre-Islamic Arabian (and later Arabic) constellation name al-qaus, "the Bow." For the pre-Islamic Arabians, al-qaus was marked by the curved line of stars ξ2, o, π, d, ρ and u Sgr (corresponding to what in other cultures was Sagittarius among the zodiacal signs). The Arabics used the indigenous name for the Greeks' Archer, alternatively translated as al-rami.

starNames.name: Magur
starNames.origin: MA2.GUR8, The Boat/Ship, is a constellation south of Sgr. It’s identification is given between Cap, Mic, CrA and southern Sgr. As certainty can only be achieved for Late Babylonian sources, WGSN picked a faint star close to the one which represents the Egyptian Boat-constellation.

starNames.name: Tusizuo
starNames.origin: Tú Sì (屠肆, "Butcher's Shop") is a Chinese asterism consisting of two stars, established by the Wuxian (巫咸) school during the Han dynasty. As "Tusi" could be confused with other celestial bodies named Tusi after two Persian astronomers (asteroid (10269) Tusi and asteroid (7058) Al-Tusi), WGSN chose to add a determinative here. The chosen star 95 Her is "the left one in Tusi", in Chinese "Tusizuo", so WGSN adopts this name.

starNames.name: Kaus Australis
starNames.origin: Arbitrarily applied in recent times, together with the Latin distinctions of "middle," "southern," and "northern" (for λ Sgr), from the pre-Islamic Arabian (and later Arabic) constellation name al-qaus, "the Bow." For the pre-Islamic Arabians, al-qaus was marked by the curved line of stars ξ2, o, π, d, ρ and u Sgr (corresponding to what in other cultures was Sagittarius among the zodiacal signs). The Arabics used the indigenous name for the Greeks' Archer, alternatively translated as al-rami.

starNames.name: Fafnir
starNames.origin: Fafnir was a Norse mythological dwarf who turned into a dragon.

starNames.name: Kaus Borealis
starNames.origin: Arbitrarily applied in recent times, together with the Latin distinctions of "middle," "southern," and "northern" (for λ Sgr), from the pre-Islamic Arabian (and later Arabic) constellation name al-qaus, "the Bow." For the pre-Islamic Arabians, al-qaus was marked by the curved line of stars ξ2, o, π, d, ρ and u Sgr (corresponding to what in other cultures was Sagittarius among the zodiacal signs). The Arabics used the indigenous name for the Greeks' Archer, alternatively translated as al-rami.

starNames.name: Bie
starNames.origin: Biē (鳖, River Turtle) is a traditional Chinese asterism. The huge cultural significance of turtles in China can be traced archaeologically to Late Hongshan culture (3300-3000 BCE).

starNames.name: Alwasl
starNames.origin: al-Waṣl (الوَصْل), “the Joint" or "Connection” is an Arabic name for the sky region between "al-Naʿām al-Wārid”, the incoming ostriches and "al-Naʿām alṢādir”, the outgoing ostriches.

starNames.name: Tianbian
starNames.origin: Tiān Biàn (Market Officer, 天弁) is a traditional Chinese asterism close to the Celestial Market super-constellation. It literally means “Celestial Cap" and describes a ceremonial headgear. The name is attested since around 100 BCE. WGSN represents it by its determinative star.

starNames.name: Vega
starNames.origin: Applied in medieval times from an abbreviation of its pre-Islamic Arabian name alnasr al-waqi', "the Swooping Eagle (or Vulture)," alternatively used as an asterism name for α, ε, and ζ Lyr. "Vega" is one of the oldest Arabic star names applied in the West, from the end of the 10th century A.D.

starNames.name: Xihe
starNames.origin: Xihe (羲和) is the goddess of the sun in the Chinese mythology and also represents the earliest astronomers and developers of calendars in ancient China.

starNames.name: Pongaponga
starNames.origin: Pongaponga (“nostrils”) is a star name from the island of Pukapuka (South Pacific) for the visual double star ε1 (4) Lyr and ε2 (5) Lyr. WGSN applies the name to ε1 Lyr A.

starNames.name: Kautoki
starNames.origin: The name means "handle (kau) of the adze (toki)" and describes an asterism from the Polynesian island of Kapingamarangi.

starNames.name: Urquchillay
starNames.origin: Urquchillay, the Llama of Many Colors, is the name of the Inka god of livestock and wildlife; it was the protector of animal. Its constellation covers large areas of Lyra; WGSN adopts the name for a star close the the god's heart.

starNames.name: Nandou
starNames.origin: Nándŏu (Southern Dipper 南斗) is a Chinese Lunar Mansion, attested for at least 2500 years: one of the oldest asterisms in China.

starNames.name: Sheliak
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Arabic constellation name al-salbaq, "the Harp," for Lyra. salbaq was a Greek loanword in Arabia, and was one of three names of musical instruments used by the Arabics for Lyra. Still other names were alsulalfat, and al-lura.

starNames.name: Ainalrami
starNames.origin: Arabic عين الرامي ʽain al-rāmī (simplified Ainalrami) means The Eye of the Archer. It originates from Arabic Almagest translations.

starNames.name: Jiantai
starNames.origin: Jiàn Tái (Clepsydra Terrace, 渐台) is a Chinese constellation of 4 stars, a symbol of astronomical timekeeping and musical pitch calibration.

starNames.name: Pabilsang
starNames.origin: Pabilsaĝ is the oldest name of the constellation Sagittarius; a Sumerian god, depicted as a mixed creature (centaur-like with additional scorpion-tail and bird features) with bow and arrow; this constellation was taken over and “simplified” by the Greeks. WGSN picked a star in his eye.

starNames.name: Nunki
starNames.origin: ᵐᵘˡNUN.KI or ᵐᵘˡNUNᴷᴵ = the star or constellation of Eridu where Eridu is one of the first big cities known. Archealogical proofs date back to the 3rd millennium (Sumer). It is located at the southern coast of Mesopotamia. The identification of the star or asterism is highly uncertain: it is often identified with Canopus and adjacent areas or "somewhere in Argo". ᵐᵘˡNUN.KI is listed in MUL.APIN and there, it seems to refer to the area of Aquarius with unknown identification (Canopus not excluded) but the identification with other Babylonian texts seems to propose only in the northern part of modern Argo, i.e. Vela. The Euphratean name "Nunki" was mentioned and associated with Sigma Sgr in Robert Brown, Jr. (1892, Proceedings of the Society of Biblical Archaeology, Volume 14, p. 298; "Nun-ki", "Prince-of-the-Earth"), and its use diffused through the 20th century after being mentioned in Richard Hinckley Allen's (Star Names, their lore and meaning, p. 359). The modern Nunki is, thus, not identical with the Sumerian one; it is one of the many misapplications.

starNames.name: Niandao
starNames.origin: Niăn Dào (Imperial Passageway, 辇道) is a private way for the emporer for harmonious journeys. WGSN represents it by its determinative star.

starNames.name: Alya
starNames.origin: From the Arabic word alya, naming the fatty tail of a breed of Eastern sheep. In Early Modern times this word was erroneously proposed as the origin of Alioth, a Medieval Latin name for ε UMa. The erroneous "Alya" was applied as a star name to θ Ser in recent times.

starNames.name: Jian
starNames.origin: Jiàn (Erect, 建) means “to set up” or “to erect,” as in raising a wooden pole or a flagstaff. It is an ancient Chinese constellation, attested since the 4th century BCE.

starNames.name: Sulafat
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Arabic constellation name al-sulabfat, "the Tortoise," for Lyra, corresponding to the Greek image of a tortoise shell for the Lyre's soundboard.

starNames.name: Arin-majlep
starNames.origin: Arin-majlep, the "replica of the Big Eye", with the Big Eye referring to Altair, is the name of a small asterism of three stars in a row: ε, ζ, and ω Aql. WGSN named ε Aql after it.

starNames.name: Ascella
starNames.origin: ascella ("armpit"). Although it appeared in the 1515 Almagest, the name does not appear to have come into common usage until the 20th century after appearing as Ascella in Richard Hinckley Allen's "Star Names Their Lore and Meaning" (1899).

starNames.name: Alqiladah
starNames.origin: al-Qilāda (القِلادَة), “the necklace”, is an Indigenous Arabian six‑star asterism recorded by al‑Ṣūfī, Ibn Qutayba, and al‑Marzūqī.

starNames.name: Okab
starNames.origin: Zeta and Epsilon Aquilae together bore the traditional name Deneb el Okab, from an Arabic term ذنب العقاب Dhanab al-ʽuqāb "the tail of the eagle".

starNames.name: Qedty
starNames.origin: Qedty (ḳdty), The Two Nets, is an Egyptian constellation, used in decan star clocks.

starNames.name: Meridiana
starNames.origin: The Latin-Arabic name "Alfecca meridiana" is mentioned in Allen (1899, 173). There, it is attributed to "Reduan" (sic!) = Ali bin Radwan's commentary to his Tetrabiblos translation (10th century). Arabic نير الفكّة nayyir al-fakka "the bright (star) of the broken (dish)" in analogy to the Arabic term for CrB. WGSN chose only the second (Latin) term: "Meridiana", the southern (one of the two Alfeccas).

starNames.name: Albaldah
starNames.origin: The name of the 21st Arabic lunar station, البلدة, Al-Baldah (The empty area), designates a starless region between ζ Sgr and α Cap; the star π Sgr is at its northern edge and was wrongly attributed with this name by Allen (1899, 359).

starNames.name: Alqubba
starNames.origin: al-Qubba (القُبَّة), “the dome or domed tent”, is an Arab asterism that correspond to the stars of Corona Australis.

starNames.name: Altais
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from a misreading of the script for the Arabic constellation name al-tinnin, "the Serpent," as it appeared incorrectly in a late Arabic star catalog, as part of the name for δ Dra. (The incorrect word, al-tais, is a real word in Arabic meaning "the He-goat," however it was never used by the pre-Islamic Arabians in stellar nomenclature. Furthermore, in the same Arabic source, in the name of ε Dra [formed parallel to that of δ Dra], the word was correctly written al-tinnin.)

starNames.name: Aladfar
starNames.origin: Aladfar derives from the Arabic الأظفر al-ʼuẓfur "the talons (of the swooping [eagle])" which designates and asterism consisting of µ and η Lyr. It was made popular by Allen.

starNames.name: Gumala
starNames.origin: Gumala is a Malay word, which means a magic bezoar stone found in snakes, dragons, etc.

starNames.name: Ninnisig
starNames.origin: Ninnisig and Erragal are two Sumerian gods associated with the pair of stars, Ninnisig is the goddess who is butcher of the highest temple (name honours a profession).

starNames.name: Kenemu
starNames.origin: (Stars of) Kenmu, 17th decan in ancient Egyptian astral science, heliacal rise in month Peret, represented by a small group of stars around rho1 Sgr.

starNames.name: Arkab Prior
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of its name for the Arabic Almagest period 'urqub al-rami, "the Archer's Achilles Tendon."

starNames.name: Arkab Posterior
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of its name for the Arabic Almagest period 'urqub al-rami, "the Archer's Achilles Tendon."

starNames.name: Rukbat
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of its name for the Arabic Almagest period rukbat al-rami, "the Archer's Knee".

starNames.name: Guqi
starNames.origin: Gŭ Qí (Drum Flag, 鼓旗) is a Chinese asterism consisting of nine stars that originated no later than about 100 BCE. It forms a super-constellation with Hé Gŭ (River-Drum) and Zuŏ Qí (Left Flag), as drums and flags were used to transmit signals.

starNames.name: Anser
starNames.origin: Johannes & Elisabetha Hevelius created “Vulpecula cum Ansere” (the Little Fox with the Goose) out of unformed stars in the space between Cygnus and Aquila. The constellation first appeared in Firmamentum Sobiescianum sive Uranographia (1687) and the accompanying introductory text, Prodromus astronomiae (1690). To emphasize that it was his own creation, Hevelius dedicated Figure L to the pair, shown as a detail in Fig. 3.1. In atlases published before Hevelius, its stars are shown simply marking the flow of the Milky Way through the area. Ian Ridpath (1989) noted that “Hevelius placed the fox near two other hunting animals, the eagle (the constellation Aquila) and the vulture (which was an alternative identification for Lyra). He explained that the fox was taking the goose to neighbouring Cerberus, another of his inventions.”unnamed before.

starNames.name: Albireo
starNames.origin: The formation of this name begins with Ptolemy's name for the constellation Cygnus - ὄρνις, "the Bird". The Arabs transliterated this name as urnis. The Medieval Latin translator of the Arabic Almagest, in turn, did not recognize any Greek word behind urnis (or whatever Arabic corruption he may have read), so he merely transliterated it into a form which appeared int he manuscripts variously as eurisim, eirisun, eirism, etc. In a note appended to this Medieval Latin constellation name for Cygnus, one Latin commentator ventured to derive it from the name of an aromatic herb he knew: ireus. This erroneous commentary read, in brief part: "eirisim...ab ireo", or, "[the constellation name] eirisim...[coming] from [the word] ireus". Apparently in one manuscript of the Latin Almagest, the final word of this commentary, ab ireo, were written on the next line below the constellation title, where the descriptions of the stars begin. Since the first star entered in the Almagest under the constellation Cygnus is β Cyg, the words ab ireo seem to have been confused as a name for this star. "Arabicized" with the insertion of the letter "l", ab ireo, written as "Albireo", was applied as a star name to β Cyg by Early Modern times.

starNames.name: Alsafi
starNames.origin: Alsafi is corrupted from Athāfi, erroneously transcribed from the Arabic plural Athāfiyy, by which the nomads designated the tripods of their open-air kitchens; one of these being imagined in σ, τ and υ [Dra].

starNames.name: Hru
starNames.origin: Hru or Ru means Arrow. The term derives from Sanskrit, but is used as a constellation on the Island of Bali for at least 1300 years.

starNames.name: Sham
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Arabic constellation name al-sahm, "the Arrow," for Sagitta.

starNames.name: Shakh
starNames.origin: ŠAḪ, Pig, is a Sumerian constellation attested in MUL.APIN (dating between 1350 and 1150 BCE). The two stars Alpha and Beta Sagittae look like the nose of the Mesopotamian constellation The Pig. WGSN applies the name to Beta.

starNames.name: Fawaris
starNames.origin: al-Fawāris (الفوارس), "the Riders" is an in indigenous Arabic asterism consisting of at least four stars. WGSN applied the name of the group to one of its members that now preserves (pars pro toto) the Indigenous heritage.

starNames.name: Tarazed
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times (with a misreading) from abbreviating the Persian asterism name shanin-i tarazu, "the Scale Beam", for α, β and γ Aql. The Persian name, in turn, was a medieval translation of these stars' Arabic name al-mizan, "the Balance".

starNames.name: Zuoqi
starNames.origin: Zuŏ Qí (Left Flag, 左旗) is a Chinese asterism consisting of nine stars and attested for more than 2000 years. It belongs to the super-constellation of flags and drums as signal transmitter. WGSN represents it by its determinative star.

starNames.name: Altair
starNames.origin: Applied with various spellings since medieval times, from an abbreviation of its Arabic name al-nars al-ta)ir, "the Flying Eagle (or Vulture)", alternatively used as an asterism name for α, β and γ Aql. The name has probable origins among the Babylonians and Sumerians, for whom α Aql was "the Eagle Star".

starNames.name: Pagru
starNames.origin: Akkadian Pagru, "body" or "corpse," is commonly translated "The Dead Man", attested as a constellation in MUL.APIN which dates between 1350 and 1150 BCE, and has been used through the entire 1st millennium BCE.

starNames.name: Libertas
starNames.origin: Libertas is Latin for "liberty". Liberty refers to social and political freedoms, and a reminder that there are people derived of liberty in the world even today. The constellation Aquila represents an eagle - a popular symbol of liberty.

starNames.name: Alshain
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times (with a misreading in the second word) from abbreviating the Persian asterism name shahin-i tarazu, "the Scale Beam," for α, β and γ Aql. The Persian name, in turn, was a medieval translation of these stars' pre-Islamic Arabian name al-mizan, "the Balance" (said to be a popular name for the pre-Islamic Arabians al-nasr al-ti'ir listed under α Aql).

starNames.name: Terebellum
starNames.origin: Ptolemy's Almagest lists four stars in a quadrilateral with ω Sgr the first in the list (the others being A, b, c Sgr). Bayer (1603) concludes this list with the note after "c": Has quatuor multi Terebellum seu τετράπλευρον vocant. A "terebellum" is an auger, so it designates the asterism at the tip of the tail and originally not a specific star.

starNames.name: Almighzal
starNames.origin: Wool Spindle – central Saudi Arabia. The constellation is used in a contemporary oral tradition by the ordinary people.

starNames.name: Telum
starNames.origin: Telum, the Dart, has been used as an alternative name for Sagitta in European literature of the past millennium (e.g. Dürer 1515, Uranometria 1603, Kepler 1627). WGSN applies the name to the brightest star of the asterism.

starNames.name: Gouguo
starNames.origin: Gŏu Guó (狗国, Territory of Dog), is a traditional Chinese asterism that corresponds to the non-Han peoples of northern and northeastern China.

starNames.name: Tianfu
starNames.origin: Tianfu (天桴) was an ancient Chinese constellation consisting of four stars. Their counting order has changed over time but we decided to take the name for the 1st star of the early (before Tang dynasty) version.

starNames.name: Antinous
starNames.origin: A "sub"-constellation (or asterism) Antinous was created by Ptolemy of Alexandria and published in the Almagest star catalogue 137 CE. It is placed in the constellation of Aquila, The Eagle.

starNames.name: Chechia
starNames.origin: Chechia is a flat-surfaced, traditional red wool hat worn by men and women, symbolising the country's rich traditions and is considered as the national headdress for in Tunisia.

starNames.name: Sukhurmashu
starNames.origin: Sukhurmashu is the Akkadian original name for this goat-fish; it was considered a benevolent and philanthropic daemon that helps humans to stay healthy and vivid.

starNames.name: Algedi
starNames.origin: Reapplied in recent times (from its older medieval spelling), from the scientific Arabic constellation name al-jady, "the Kid," for Capricornus.

starNames.name: Alshat
starNames.origin: The Arabic term سعد الذابح, Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ, The Lucky Asterism of the Slaughterer (22 lunar station), consists of the 3 stars: α1, β and ν Cap. As α and β already have proper names, the corrupted form "shat" (for sad) was used to name ν Cap.

starNames.name: Dabih
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the pre-Islamic Arabian lunar mansion name sa'd aldhabih, for α and β Cap. Possible meanings for the name are "the Lucky (Stars) of the Slaughterer," or, "Sa'd, the Slaughtering One" (this last using Sa'd as an unspecified proper name). However the exact historical connections are unknown.

starNames.name: Sadr
starNames.origin: "Breast" in Arabic

starNames.name: Peacock
starNames.origin: Invented for The Air Almanac of the HM Nautical Almanac Office

starNames.name: Aldulfin
starNames.origin: Arabic scholarship adopted the Greek loanword "dulfim" or "dulfin" (with article: ad-dulfin or simplified adulfin) for the marine mammal. The star ε Del at the dorsal fin of the Ptolemaic (smaller than ancient Greek) figure was called Al Dhanab al Dulfim (the Dolphin's Tail) and as there are many stars named with the Arabic root for "tail", WGSN adopted only the last part of the name.

starNames.name: Rotanev
starNames.origin: Nicolaus Venator, responsible for 1814 star catalogue)

starNames.name: Sualocin
starNames.origin: reversed Latin Nicolaus Venator, responsible for 1814 star catalogue)

starNames.name: Deneb
starNames.origin: "Tail" in Arabic

starNames.name: Aljanah
starNames.origin: The star used to be commonly named Gienah (cf. Kunitzsch and Smart 2006, Allen 1899) which derives from Arabic al-Janāḥ, The Wing, based on Almagest translations. WGSN adopted the original Arabic word instead of the corrupted one.

starNames.name: Dhanishta
starNames.origin: one of the Nakshatras, a constellation, depicted as an (unnumbered) multitude of stars

starNames.name: Albali
starNames.origin: From the Arabic word bali(, "swallower", used in an Arabic discussion pertaining to the Arabic lunar mansion name sa(d bula( (given for ε, μ and ν Aqr; of unknown meaning). In recent times the Arabic article al- was added to bali( and the word was applied as a star name.

starNames.name: Musica
starNames.origin: Musica is Latin for "music".

starNames.name: Udang
starNames.origin: Udang, "the Shrimp", is an Oceanic name from Bali (Indonesia). It is anchored in the cultural calendar called "Palelintangan" which is attested for ~1300 years. Particularly whiteleg and tiger shrimp are leading fishery commodity in Bali with significant economic potential.

starNames.name: Polaris Australis
starNames.origin: the term literally means "South Pole" and was first used for the star in the 18th century.

starNames.name: Protome
starNames.origin: Protome, the Bust, is the original name of this constellation from Roman time when Greek was still the language of science. The reasons for this invention are not preserved, but mythology later added.

starNames.name: Tianjinnan
starNames.origin: “Southern star of Tianjin”, the Celestial Ferry, is in the Chinese constellation that allows is celebrated to allow the celestial couple of The Girl and The Cowherd to meet once a year.

starNames.name: Tepennekhet
starNames.origin: Head of the Giant, the Giant (Nekhet) being an important Egyptian constellation, is a star name from the Ramesside Star Clocks (1400 and 1200 BCE).

starNames.name: Enduri Senggu
starNames.origin: Name of the Hedgehog Goddess. She is the guardian of human dwellings and in the sky points head northwards, tail southwards in winter.

starNames.name: Kitalpha
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Arabic constellation name qit'at al-faras, "the Section of the Horse," for Equuleus. Ptolemy had Ἵππου Προτομή, "the First Half of the Horse," for the constellation, because it shows only half the figure (as with the constellations Taurus, Pegasus, and the Greek ship Argo).

starNames.name: Aerostaticus
starNames.origin: Globus Aerostaticus is one of the obsolete constellations, introduced in early modern time to celebrate new technologies.

starNames.name: Alderamin
starNames.origin: Applied to α Cep since medieval times. The erroneous derivation understood since Early Modern times was from al-dhira (al-)yamin, "the Right Forearm," an assumed Arabic descriptive term for α Cep. Firstly, in the Almagest, α Cep is described on the right "shoulder" (Arabic al-katif or al-mankib) of Cepheus, whereas no right "forearm" (al-dhira<) is described for the figure. Secondly, in Arabic, "right forearm" is spelled correctly as al-dhira al-yumna, which (in contrast to al-yamin) lacks assonance in the last syllable to Alderamin. Therefore, it is more likely that Alderamin is derived from the various medieval Christian abbreviations of muqaddam al-dhira<ain, "the Preceding One of the Two Cubits, or Forearms," which was a name for the Arabic Almagest period (based on pre-Islamic Arabian) for α Gem. This would have been wrongly transferred to α Cep in medieval times.

starNames.name: Alfirk
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of the pre-Islamic Arabian names kaukaba al-firq (for α and β Cep ), and kawakib al-firq (for α, β , and η Cep). kaukaba and kawakib mean "two stars" and "stars" (more than two), respectively, but the original Arabic script for al-firq can be vocalized in various ways with various meanings. If the vocalization al-firq is accepted, it means "the Flock," and may refer to a flock of sheep here.

starNames.name: Sadalsuud
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Arabic lunar mansion name sa(d al-su(ud, for β and ξ Aqr, and 46 Cap. A possible meaning for the name is "the Luckiest of the Lucky (Stars)", but the exact historical connections are unknown.

starNames.name: Bunda
starNames.origin: Bunda is a Persian lunar mansion.

starNames.name: Nashira
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the pre-Islamic Arabian name sa<d nashira, for γ and δ Cap. Its meaning is unknown. As originally applied, γ was "Nashira Prima" and δ was "Nashira Posterior."

starNames.name: Azelfafage
starNames.origin: From the Arabic constellation name al-sulahfat, "the Tortoise," for Lyra ( corresponding to the Greek image of a tortoise shell for the Lyre's soundboard). Transliterated as Azelfage, a Medieval Latin translator erroneously attributed this constellation name to Cygnus. Then in Early Modern times, the corruption "Azelfafage" was applied as a star name to π1 Cyg.

starNames.name: Garnet Star
starNames.origin: Piazzi (1803) named the star Garnet Sidus due to a description by W. Herschel (1773) as "deep garnet red"; the English name is well-established in recent literature and textbooks.

starNames.name: Enif
starNames.origin: Applied in medieval times, evidently from the Arabic word anf, "nose" (Ptolemy had described this star on the horse's "muzzle"). However, Arabic sources do not mention anf for ε Peg, only other terms, hence the ultimate origin of "Enif" remains uncertain.

starNames.name: Baijiu
starNames.origin: Bài Jiù (Broken Mortar, 敗臼) is a Chinese asterism of four stars that represents damaged implement for processing staple food.

starNames.name: Deneb Algedi
starNames.origin: "Tail of the Goat" in Arabic

starNames.name: Aldhanab
starNames.origin: Al Dhanab from Arabic ال ذنب (adh-dhanab), The Tail, became common since its mentioning in Allen (1899). There it is attributed to a Persian astronomer but the whole constellation Grus is a constellation invented in the Early Modern Era.

starNames.name: Kurhah
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from one vocalization of its pre-Islamic Arabian name: al-qurha, "the White Spot on the Forehead of a Horse." However, the original Arabic script for the name can be read and vocalized in other ways with various meanings.

starNames.name: Sadalmelik
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Arabic name sa(d al-malik, for α and ο Aqr. A possible meaning for the name is "the Lucky (Stars) of the King", but the exact historical connections are unknown.

starNames.name: Jiu
starNames.origin: Jiù (Mortar, 臼) and Nèichŭ (Inner Pestle, 內杵) are a Chinese super-constellation attested since Han Dynasty.

starNames.name: Alnair
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of its late Arabic name al-nayyir min dhanab al-but, "the Bright One from the Fish's Tail" (where a l6th century Arabic astronomer had extended Ptolemy's Southern Fish [Piscis Austrinus] into what is today Grus). The form Al Na'ir was taken from a wrong transliteration (Al Na'ir) of the Arabic adjective al-nayyir, "the Bright One."

starNames.name: Neichu
starNames.origin: Nèichŭ (Inner Pestle, 內杵) is a three-star Chinese asterism that forms a super-constellation with Jiù (Mortar, 臼); they are attested for more than 2000 years.

starNames.name: Biham
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of the pre-Islamic Arabian name sa'd al-biham, for θ and ν Peg. A possible meaning for the name is "the Lucky (Stars) of the Young Beasts [lambs, kids, and the like]," but the exact historical connections are unknown.

starNames.name: Ancha
starNames.origin: A Latin word meaning "hip", used in the Medieval Latin Almagest in describing σ and ι/38 Aqr in the right and left hips, respectively (following an error, for Ptolemy had these stars in "the buttocks"). The word was applied as a star name to θ Aqr (correctly in Ptolemy's "right socket of the hip") in recent times.

starNames.name: Lang-Exster
starNames.origin: "Lang" is an Malayan/ Indonesian term meaning "hornbill", "Exster" is a Dutch word meaning "magpie" and both terms were used as name for the newly defined constellation in Early Modern Age by the Dutch sailors (de Houtman 1603) who artificially created the constellation as "Indian Magpie" referring to a species of bird with a strong cultural significance for the indigenous people they met (e.g. Dayak). The star is a spectroscopic binary which is why it makes sense to give it a double-name for the visible dot; the name may be split for the components later.

starNames.name: Sadachbia
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the Arabic lunar mansion name sa(d al-akhbiya, for γ, π, ζ and η Aqr. A possible meaning for the name is "the Lucky (Stars) of the Tents", but the exact historical connections are unknown.

starNames.name: Alsamaka
starNames.origin: Al-Samaka al-Ṣuġrā (Arabic: السمكة الصغرى, The Smaller Fish) is an Arabic asterism in Lacerta and Andromeda, attested since Ibn Qutayba.

starNames.name: Stellio
starNames.origin: Hevelius, who invented the constellation Lacerta sive Stellio (modern Lacerta), gave it the alternative name Stellio in his star catalogue and atlas.

starNames.name: Tiangang
starNames.origin: Tiān Gāng (天綱, Celestial Rope) is a traditional Chinese constellation that represents large ropes used to pitch tents — and symbolically represents the Celestial Military Tent of the emperor on campaign.

starNames.name: Fenmu
starNames.origin: Fén Mù (Tomb, 墳墓) is an ancient Chinese constellation. The cluster of constellations with that topic can be understood as a celestial projection of funeral rituals.

starNames.name: Situla
starNames.origin: A Latin word meaning "pot" or "bucket", used in Early Modern philological studies as the translation of the Arabic constellation name al-dalw, for Aquarius. Subsequently the word was applied as a star name to k Aqr. The Arabs located al-dalw ("the Well Bucket") in today's Square of Pegasus. In that location it corresponded to what in other cultures was Aquarius among the zodiacal signs. The Arabs subsequently used the indigenous name al-dalw for the Greek Water Pourer (Aquarius).

starNames.name: Homam
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of the pre-Islamic Arabian name sa'd al-humam, for ζ and ξ Peg. A possible meaning for the name is "the Lucky (Stars) of the Hero," but the exact historical connections are unknown.

starNames.name: Tiaki
starNames.origin: Makemson (1941: 261 #659) lists Tiaki as the Tuamotuan name for β Gru, sourcing this to unpublished field data supplied by Kenneth P. Emory (ibid.: 197). However, Emory's star information does not appear in his later publications and has not been located to date in archives of his unpublished material. Stimson's Tuamotuan dictionary (1964: 526) gives the meaning of Tīaki as "guardian", "keeper" or "watchman", but does not list it as a star. He does, however, list Tīakitau as the name of an unidentified star on Anaa, which Makemson (1941: 261 #660) lists separately.

starNames.name: Matar
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from an abbreviation of the pre-Islamic Arabian name sa'd matar for η and o Peg. Its meaning is unknown. matar has been translated as "rain," and as a common noun in Arabic, al-matar does mean "the rain." However, lack of the definitive article al- for the star points to a use of the word in a sense different from the common noun.

starNames.name: Ligong
starNames.origin: Ligong (離宮) denoted a secondary or temporary palace situated apart from the principal palace and used for the ruler’s temporary residence, repose, and private life.

starNames.name: Tugongli
starNames.origin: Tŭ Gōng Lì (Clerks of the Earth Official, 土公吏) is an ancient Chinese two-star asterism.

starNames.name: Lintangkumba
starNames.origin: Lintang in Bahasa Indonesia means asterism; 'kumba' in Balinese is a vessel with sacred water; it derives from Sanskrit कुम्भ (kumbha), jar or pitcher. In both Indian and Indonesian cultures, it is a name for the constellation in Aquarius. In India, it also designates the rāśi (zodiac sign).

starNames.name: Sadalbari
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from the pre-Islamic Arabian name sa'd al-bari', for λ and μ Peg. A possible meaning for the name is "the Lucky (Stars) of the Excelling One," but the exact historical connections are unknown.

starNames.name: Shatabhisha
starNames.origin: Śatabhiṣa (शतभिष), literally "hundred physicians", is the name of the 24th nakshatra of Vedic astronomy. Its earliest attestation is in a Vedic religious text (Atharvaveda) from the first millennium BCE, and an astronomy text (Vedanga Jyotisha) that dates around 300 BCE. As the yogatara (main star) of this nakshatra, λ Aquarii stands "pars pro toto" for the entire constellation.

starNames.name: Skat
starNames.origin: Applied with various spellings since medieval times, from the Arabic word al-saq, "the shin", used in the Arabic Almagest in describing this star.

starNames.name: Leidian
starNames.origin: Léi Diàn (Thunder and Lightning, 雷電) is a Chinese constellation that is so called because it vanishes as soon as it appears; it has no correlation with meteorology.

starNames.name: Tengshe
starNames.origin: Tengshe螣蛇 or 腾蛇 (Téng Shé, Flying Serpent) is a constellation created by ancient Chinese astrologers, dating back to the 2nd century BCE.

starNames.name: Helvetios
starNames.origin: Helvetios is the Latin for "the Helvetian" and refers to the Celtic tribe that lived in Switzerland during the Middle Ages.

starNames.name: Fomalhaut
starNames.origin: Applied with various spellings since medieval times, from an abbreviation of its name for the Arabic Almagest period fam al-but al-janubi, "the Mouth of the Southern Fish."

starNames.name: Alfarasalkamil
starNames.origin: Alfarasalkamil (الفرس الكامل) means "The Complete Horse", as opposed to the Greek constellation of a half horse that is now called Pegasus. The Arabian tradition may perhaps root in or connect to the Babylonian one.

starNames.name: Scheat
starNames.origin: From the Arabic word al-saq, "the shin," used in the Arabic Almagest in describing δ Aqr. Wrongly transferred as a star name to β Peg in late medieval times.

starNames.name: Fumalsamakah
starNames.origin: Arabic فم السمكة fum al-samakah means "mouth of the fish". The name was considered traditional by the IAU in 2016, although it does not appear in Kunitzsch and Smart (2006) and not in Allen (1899).

starNames.name: Markab
starNames.origin: From an abbreviation of the name for the Arabic Almagest period mankib al-faras, "the Horse's Shoulder," for β Peg. Wrongly transferred to α Peg in late medieval times.

starNames.name: Safina
starNames.origin: an Indigenous Arabic constellation of the Ship was between Diphda and Fomalhaut (see al Qutayba); WGSN picked one of the possible stars in the area. considering the close vicinity of the Greek star name "Hydor" (The Water) north of it, it becomes a sunken treasure ship.

starNames.name: Honores
starNames.origin: The Latin term "Honores" means honour. A constellation introduced by Bode (1801). He had given a paper in 1790 that this was a joined decision by many European astronomers as a memorial to an extraordinarily generous patron of scientific research and benevolent, peaceful ruler. WGSN considers this message worth to convay even without the dedication to a specific person; we named a star in the feather "Honores" as there is a German proverb "Die Feder ist mächtiger als das Schwert" (the feather is mightier than the sword).

starNames.name: Yunyu
starNames.origin: Yún Yǔ (Cloud and Rain, 雲雨) is a four-star Chinese asterism which forms a super-constellation with Pili and Leidian; it is associated with plentiful, auspicious rainfall and the flourishing of plants. They have been documented for at least 2000 years.

starNames.name: Salm
starNames.origin: Bayer (1603) mentions three names: Markab, Sagma and its corruption Salma. Allen (1899, 329) considers the correct form "Salm", a Leathern Bucket.

starNames.name: Alkarab
starNames.origin: traditional Arabic name Al Karab, The Bucket-rope, was an asterism consisting of τ and υ Peg

starNames.name: Veritate
starNames.origin: From the latin "Veritas", truth. The ablative form means "where there is truth".

starNames.name: Udkadua
starNames.origin: The Sumerian term UD.KA.DU8.A is a compound, literally meaning "the storm demon with the gaping mouth". This Babylonian constellation is at least 3000 years old; the star named after it is its heel. It was highly important, as it was used for time-measurement for at least a millennium (if not longer).

starNames.name: Rasalnaqa
starNames.origin: The group of stars that Ptolemy called "The Hand of Andromeda" is also called "The Head of the She-Camel" in an Indigenous Arabian tradition. as-Sufi (11th c. CE) combines these two traditions, and so does IAU by naming one of the star after "the hand" and the other one "the camel's head"

starNames.name: Errai
starNames.origin: Applied in recent times from its pre-Islamic Arabian name al-ra'i, "the Shepherd". This shepherd, with the sheep he attended (al-aghnam, marked by the various dim stars nearby), and the shepherd's dog (kalb al-ra'i,marked by 28/29 [ρ] Cep), seem to form a complete group of pre-Islamic Arabian figures.

starNames.name: Puwuh Atarung
starNames.origin: Puwuh Atarung (ᬧᬸᬯᬸᬄᬳᬢᬭᬸᬂ) means "battling quails", birds that are crucial poultry source of nutritious animal protein (meat and eggs). Their constellation has been used on Bali since 700 CE.

starNames.name: Kaffalmusalsala
starNames.origin: Arabic desciption of a Greek star name. The Arabic term (كفّ المسلسة) means "Hand of the Chained Woman"; originating from the Almagest "Hand of Andromeda", originally designating a group of three stars.

starNames.name: Pili
starNames.origin: Pī Lì (Thunderbolt, 霹靂) is a five-star Chinese constellation, which forms a super-constellation with Yunyu (clouds & rain) and Leidian (thunder and lightning).
